speechtext: Just in answer to one question, I am familiar with the fact to which the right hon. gentleman has referred, w'ith the provisions of the Lord's Day Act to be embodied in a statute founded on the approval of this convention. But the Lord's Day Act does not go quite as far as this convention does in connection with cases in which the day of rest could not be the Lord's Day. For instance, I know of cases that came to my attention within the last few months in which men have been working continuously seven days a week without any day of rest and this convention does not contemplate that being done. Intimation of the existing legislation has been given to the international labour office as the right hon. gentleman has said, in more than one case. In fact, sometimes when during my tenure of office cables have come for information relating to a particular matter one is able to refer to statutes in one's own statute books, but it does not come within either approval or ratification so far as the convention itself is concerned if there is a difference in details between the convention and our legislation, and in order that there may be no question we have gone a step further than merely advising them; we have asked the approval of this house to this draft convention.

Convention Limiting the Hours of Work in Industrial Undertakings to Eight in the Day and Forty-eight in the Week The general conference of the international labour organization of the League of Nations,

adopts the following draft convention for ratification by the members of the international labour organization, in accordance with the labour part of the treaty of Versailles of 28 June, 1919, and of the treaty of St. Germain of 10 September, 1919:
Article 1.-For the purpose of this convention, the term "industrial undertaking" includes particularly:
(a)	Mines, quarries, and other works for the extraction of minerals from the earth.
(b)	Industries in which articles are manufactured, altered, cleaned, repaired, ornamented, finished, adapted for sales, broken up or demolished, or in which materials are transformed; including shipbuilding and the generation, transformation, and transmission of electricity or motive power of any kind.
(c)	Construction, reconstruction, maintenance, repair, alteration, or demolition of any building, railway, tramway, harbour, dock, pier, canal, inland waterway, road, tunnel, bridge, viaduct, sewer, drain, well, telegraphic or telephonic installation, electrical undertaking, gas work, waterwork or other work of construction, as well as the preparation for or laying the foundations of any such work or structure.
(d)	Transport of passengers or goods by road, rail, sea or inland waterway, including the handling of goods at docks, quays, wharves or warehouses, but excluding transport by hand.
The provisions relative to transport by sea and on inland waterways shall be determined by a special conference dealing with employment at sea and on inland waterways.
The competent authority in each country shall define the line of division which separates industry from commerce and agriculture.
Article 2.-The working hours of persons employed in any public or private undertaking or in any branch thereof, other than an undertaking in which only members of the same family are employed, shall not exceed eight in the day and forty-eight in the week, with the exceptions hereinafter provided for.
(a)	The provisions of this convention shall not apply to persons holding positions of supervision or management, nor to persons employed in a confidential capacity.
(b)	Where by law, custom, or agreement between employers' and worked organizations, or, where no such organizations exist, between employers' and workers' representatives, the hours of work on one or more days of the week are less than eight, the limit of eight hours may be exceeded on the remaining day6 of the week by the sanction of the competent public authority, or by agreement between such organizations or representatives; provided, however, that in no case under the provisions of this paragraph shall the daily limit of eight hours be exceeded by more than one hour.
(c)	Where persons are employed in shifts it shall be permissible to employ persons in excess of eight hours in any one day and forty-eight hours in any one week, if the average number of hours over a period of three weeks or less does not exceed eight per day and forty-eight per week.
Article 3.-The limit of hours of work prescribed in article 2 may be exceeded in case of accident, actual or threatened, or in case of urgent work to be done to machinery or plant, or in case of "force majeure," but only so far as may be necessary to avoid serious interference with the ordinary working of the undertaking.
Article 4.-The limit of hours of work prescribed in article 2 may also be exceeded in those processes which are required by reason of the nature of the process to be carried on continuously by a succession of shifts, subject to the condition that the working hours shall not exceed fifty-six in the week on the average. Such regulation of the hours of work shall in no case affect any rest days which may be secured by the national law to the workers in such processes in compensation for the weekly rest day.
Article 5.-In exceptional cases where it is recognized that the provisions of article 2 cannot be applied, but only in such cases, agreeimente between workers' and employers' organizations concerning the daily limit of work over a longer period of time may be given the force of regulations, if the government, to which these agreements shall be submitted, so decides.
The average number of hours worked per week, over the number of weeks covered by any such agreement shall not exceed forty-eight.
Article 6.-Regulations made by public authority shall determine for industrial undertakings:
(a)	The permanent exceptions that may be allowed in preparatory or complementary work which must necessarily be carried on outside the limits laid down for the general working of an establishment, or for certain classes of workers whose work is essentially intermittent.
(b)	The temporary exceptions that may be allowed, so that establishments may deal with exceptional cases of pressure of work.
These regulations shall be made only after consultation with the organizations of employers and workers concerned, if any such organizations exist. These regulations shall fix the maximum of additional hours in each instance, and the rate of pay for overtime shall not be less than one and one-quarter times the regular rate.
Article 7.-Each government shall communicate to the international labour office:
(a)	A list of the processes which are classed as being necessarily continuous in character under article 4;
lb) hull information as to working of the agreements mentioned in article 5; and
IcJ hull information concerning the regulations made under article 6 and their application.
The international labour office shall make an annual report thereon to the general conference of the international labour Organization.
Article 8.-In order to facilitate the enforcement of the provisions of this convention, every employer shall be required:
la) To notify by means of the posting of notices in conspicuous places in the works or other suitable place, or by such other method as may be approved by the government, the hours at which work begins and ends, and where work is carried on by shifts, the hours at which each shift begins and ends. These hours shall be so fixed that the duration of the work shall not exceed the limits prescribed by this convention, and when so notified they shall not be changed except with such notice and in such manner as may be approved by the government.
(b)	To notify in the same way such rest intervals accorded during the period of work as are not reckoned as part of the working hours.
(c)	To keep a record in the form prescribed by law or regulation in each country of all additional hours worked in pursuance of articles 3 and 6 of this convention.

Now, sir, bearing in mind that article and a further article, namely 427, we submit with complete confidence that this is within the legislative competence of the parliament of Canada. Article 427 sets forth the general principles that govern, and reads as follows:
The high contracting parties, recognizing that the well-being, physical, moral and intellectual, of industrial wage-earners is of supreme international importance, have framed, in order to further this great end, the permanent machinery provided for in section 1 and' associated with that of the League of Nations.
They recognize that differences of climate, habits and customs, of economic opportunity and industrial tradition, make strict uniformity in the conditions of labour difficult of immediate attainment. But, holding as they do, that labour should not be regarded merely as an article of commerce, they think that there are methods and principles for regulating labour conditions which all industrial communities should endeavour to apply, so far as their special circumstances will permit.
Among these method's and principles, the following seem to the high contracting parties to be of special and urgent importance:
First-The guiding principle above enunciated that labour should not be regarded merely as a commodity or article of commerce.
Second-The right of association for all lawful purposes by the employed as well as by the employers.

Third-The payment to the employed of a wage adequate to maintain a reasonable standard of life as this is understood in their time and country.
Fourth-The adoption of an eight hour day or a forty-eight hour week as the standard to be aimed at where it has not already been attained.
Fifth-The adoption of a weekly rest of at least twenty-four hours, which should include Sunday wherever practicable.
Sixth-The abolition of child labour and the imposition of such limitations on the labour of young persons as shall permit the continuation of their education and assure their proper physical development.
Seventh-The principle that men and women should receive equal remuneration for work of equal value.
Eighth-The standard set by law in each country with respect to the conditions of labour should have due regard to the equitable economic treatment of all workers lawfully resident therein.
Ninth-Each state should make provision for a system of inspection in which women should take part, in order to ensure the enforcement of the laws and regulations for the protection of the employed.
Without claiming that these methods and principles are either complete or final, the high contracting parties arc of opinion that they are well fitted to guide the policy of the League of Nations; and that, if adopted by the industrial communities who are members of the league, and safeguarded in practice by an adequate system of such inspection, they will confer lasting benefits upon the wage-earners of the world.

It is important to bear in mind that an international treaty not only involves the acceptance of obligations; it must be taken to confer benefits as well. The obligations are with respect to other countries; the privileges are the benefits that, by the signature of other countries, we enjoy in consequence of their having become parties to the treaty. So there is a measure of mutuality and benefit conferred on each country by all the others, and when you have an important treaty, an international obligation signed by practically all the nations of the world in the manner in which this treaty was signed, conferring benefits, privileges and advantages by each country upon the other, with each country on the other hand accepting the obligations and responsibilities that are incident to the execution of such a document, you should have practically an ideal instrument so far as international relations are concerned.
I pointed out that there was a clear recognition on the part of those who made the treaty that there were varjdng forms of government in the countries of the world. The unitary form of government presented no difficulties, for the parliament of that particular country could deal with every matter that might arise for consideration. For instance, the parliament of the United Kingdom deals with matters touching the water works of cities such as Birmingham and Manchester; with local government in small areas and communities; with parish rates and poor law rates, and also with the great problems of defence of its territory on sea and land and with questions of foreign policy concerning disarmament and the peace

of the world. So a unitary system of government need have no limitations of any kind imposed upon it. But where you have a federal union or a federated state you must look to the instrument that created the state and to the constitution under which it operates to determine the extent of the power to be exercised by each of the units that comprise the state itself, and the power conferred by the constitution on the central authority.
It is important, therefore, to consider what powers have been given our provinces and what legislative juridiction has been conferred upon the central power. I do not propose this afternoon to enter into any lengthy argument in this regard, beyond saying that broadly and generally matters of a local nature are within the jurisdiction of the provinces, notably matters in connection with property and civil rights and other matters such as education, subject to limitations, and certain questions with respect to agriculture subject to the supreme power of the dominion parliament if it is exercised over the same subject matter, and questions of that kind. But when we deal with section 91 of the British North America Act we have an entirely different matter to consider. That section confers upon the parliament of Canada exclusive power to legislate for the dominion as a whole. The legislation, indeed, is prefaced by the words with which this parliament is so familiar, that is, the general term peace, order and good government for the whole of Canada, and the succeeding division of the powers by section 91 illustrates the subjects that have to be considered as indicative of the exercise of power with respect to peace, order and good government. I need not take time to run through them, because they are very familiar to every hon. member of this house. TVe are constantly exercising them. They relate to banks and banking; navigation and shipping; copyrights; bankruptcy; interest; legal tender; savings banks; weights and measures; sea coast and inland fisheries; postal service; the census and statistics, and matters of that kind. Therefore under our constitution which we familiarly refer to as the British North America Act, we have exclusive jurisdiction-and I should like hon. members of the house to bear in mind that the word is "exclusive"-conferred upon the legislatures of the several provinces, the words being:
In each province the legislature may exclusively make laws in relation to matters coming within the classes of subjects next hereinafter enumerated; that is to say-
Then the closing sub-head, No. 16, reads:
Generally all matters of a merely local or private nature in the province.

I am coming to that. The provincial power is exclusive, and I read the -words contained in paragraph 16 of section 92 for the purpose of making it clear that the broad and general provision of the statute is that matters generally of a local nature in the provinces shall be within the jurisdiction of the legislatures. But when we come to deal with section 91, which as I said is the section that confers powers upon this parliament, it will be found that the words are as follows:
It shall be lawful for the Queen, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons, to make laws for the peace, order and good government of Canada, in relation to all matters not coming within the classes of subjects by this act assigned exclusively to the legislatures of the provinces-
And for greater certainty certain subjects are mentioned, such as I indicated a few moments ago. Obviously to interpret those two sections is a matter of great difficulty. You have to rely upon judicial decisions, because the point at which there may be, shall I say, an interference with the fullest exercise of its powers by a provincial legislature, by legislation of the dominion parliament, is very difficult to determine. Therefore we have a long line of judicial decisions determining the extent to which the powers of the legislatures might be exclusively exercised and the subjects over which this central parliament has power, to the exclusion of jurisdiction on the part of the provinces. We have had many difficult cases before the courts. If I were asked what I thought was the greatest service rendered to Canada by the judicial committee of the privy council I would say it was found in the fact that there can be but one judgment in that tribunal. It is not a judgment in the narrow sense of the term; it is the advice which that committee of the king's council gives to the sovereign as to how differences should be adjudicated between his subjects or between those who are litigating, sometimes not his subjects, in his courts. As there is no such

International Labour Conventions
thing as a dissenting judgment in that committee; as there is no possibility of there being two opinions, strong though may be the differences of opinion between the individuals during the progress of the argument or even at its conclusion; as there must be but one judgment embodying the recommendation made to the sovereign as to how the matter in question should be disposed of, I believe that makes for a measure of harmony that otherwise would be denied. Consider, for instance, the many judgments of the Supreme Court of Canada in which sometimes acute legal differences all unconsciously have brought about a division of opinion, with two members of the court finding one way and three members another, or four members finding one way and one member another. It will be recalled also that in that very vital moment in the history of the United States when the question of the validity of an election for the presidency was under consideration, the supreme court of that country divided sharply upon political lines, and it was many years before the country recovered from the shock that the public conscience received by reason of the judgment then delivered.
So I believe that one of the greatest services, if not the greatest service, rendered to this country has been that the court of last resort, the judicial committee of the privy council, in arriving at its recommendations to the sovereign as to how matters should be determined that have called for the interpretation of our constitution, has been the fact that there can be only one recommendation. I think that has been one of the greatest safeguards of our daily life. Obviously I do not propose this afternoon to address hon. members of this house as though they were a court, because that would be unfair both to them and to myself. In my own simple way I should like to indicate to hon. members the principles which during the progress of the years have been evolved to enable legislatures and parliaments properly to deal with matters which come before them for consideration.
Only a few moments ago the right hon. leader of the opposition referred to the reference made to the Supreme Court of Canada by the government of the day with respect to the constitutionality of the provision in our law which deals with hours of labour. The report of the case will be found in the 1925 Supreme Court reports, commencing at page 505. I ask the house to bear in mind the date of that decision. As I have said it was in 1925. The case was argued on June 11
and on June 18 of that year judgment was given. I think it would be well to read the questions because they may be useful to hon. members who wish to discuss the matter. The questions submitted to the court were as follows :
(1)	What is the nature of the obligation of the Dominion of Canada as a member of the international labour conference, under the provisions of the labour part (Part XIII) of the treaty of Versailles and of the corresponding provisions of the other treaties of peace, with relation to such draft conventions and recommendations as may be from time to time adopted by the said conference under the authority of and pursuant to the aforesaid provisions?
(2)	Are the legislatures of the provinces the authorities within whose competence the subject matter of the said draft convention (Copy of which is herewith submitted) in whole or in part lies and before whom such draft convention should be brought, under the provisions of Article 405 of the treaty of peace with Germany, for the enactment of legislation or other action?
(3)	If the subject matter of the said draft
convention be, in part only, within the competence of the legislatures of the provinces, then in what particular or particulars, or to what extent, is the subject matter of the draft convention within the competence of the legislatures?	.
(4)	If the subject matter of the said draft convention be, in part only, within the competence of the legislatures of the provinces, then in what particular or particulars, or to what extent, is the subject matter of the draft convention within the competence of the parliament of Canada?
The unanimous decision of the court was given by Mr. Justice, now Chief Justice Duff, and the questions were answered as follows:
To the first question: the obligation is simply in the nature of an undertaking to bring the recommendation or draft convention before the authority or authorities within whose competence the matter lies, for the enactment of legislation or other action. A
To the second question: Yes, in part.
To the third question: The subject matter is generally within the competence of the legislatures of the provinces, but the authority vested in these legislatures does not enable them to give the force of law to provisions such as those contained in the draft convention in relation to servants of the dominion government, or to legislate for those parts of Canada which are not within the boundaries of a province.
To the fourth question: The parliament of Canada has exclusive legislative authority in those parts of Canada not within the boundaries of any province, and also upon the subjects dealt with in the draft convention in relation to the servants of the dominion government.
The sense, therefore, of the answers to the questions as they appear at page 512 of the report is that there was no obligation upon the dominion parliament to enact legislation, and that the federal power had discharged its

International Labour Conventions
duty when it submitted to the provincial legislatures, through dispatches to the lieutenant governors, the matters tliat were within the exclusive jurisdiction of the provincial legislatures. There is one observation found at pages 510 and 511 in the judgment of Mr. Justice Duff to which I should like to refer:
It seems questionable whether government employees, in industrial undertakings carried on by the government, such, for example, as shipbuilding, are within the scope of the convention. The point was not the subject of argument before us, and concerning it no opinion is intended to be expressed.
It is necessary to observe, also, that as regards those parts of Canada which are not included within the limits of any province, the legislative authority in relation to civil rights generally, and to the subject matter of the convention in particular, is the dominion parliament.
Then after further discussion he gave the answers to the questions I have just read. That was in 1925. The development of our constitutional power by judicial decisions is of course not a static thing; there is constant movement and progress. Different judges have taken different views, and undoubtedly, as Mr. Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes has said, the state of .public opinion, generally, influences judicial decisions not to the extent of in any sense modifying precedents, but expanding in every possible way the meaning to be given to language to meet the new conditions under which people may live. Perhaps the most striking example of that is to be found in the decision given in the House of Lords in connection with trade conspiracies, f refer to Allen and Flood. The method by vhieh our common law has expanded to meet ;he demands made upon it by new conditions n our civilization is I think, as the late Mr. lustice Macready in England said, one of the most remarkable circumstances of our civilization.
But the interpretation of a statute is an mtirely different matter from the adjudication nf differences between litigants. Rules of construction have been framed during all the years, and the method to be applied in dealing with a given statute has usually become more or less settled by long practice and the passage of time. Only a few days ago my colleague, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) read to this chamber a summary of the rules which the present Lord Chancellor of England said he regarded as the general principles to be taken from a perusal of the cases. I need hardly point out to hon. members that over a period of sixty years it is quite impossible to say that complete consistency has governed

in the adjudication of various men who have dealt with the British North America Act. For instance, there was a day when under the strong and dominating influence of Lord Watson the swing of the pendulum was towards the maintenance, at the expense of federal power, of the provincial authorities. I need hardly say there was a relaxation of that condition, and in later years there was a saving towards the supremacy of the federal power. Particularly was that so when the events of the great war indicated how essential it was that there should be a strong law making authority, or that power should be in the central authority.
Perhaps before dealing with that point it might be desirable, for the purpose of making it part of my observations, to read the rules to which Lord Sankey has referred, because they may be of value to some hon. members who will read what is taking place this afternoon. He has said this:
While the decisions which the board has pronounced in the many constitutional cases which have come under their consideration from the dominion must each be regarded in the light of the facts involved in it. their lordships recognize that there has grown up round the British North America Act a body of precedents of high authority and value as guides to its interpretation and application. The useful and essential task of taking stock of this body of authority and reviewing it in relation to the original text has been undertaken by this board from time to time and notably, for example, in the cases of Attorney General of Ontario v. Attorney General of Canada and others; Attorney General for Canada v. Attorneys General for the provinces of Ontario, Quebec, and Nova Scotia: city of Montreal v. Montreal Street Railway Company, and in the same year Attorney General for Ontario and others v. Attorney General for Canada and another. In all these four cases the scope of the two sections was carefully considered, but it is not necessary to cite them at length because so recently as last year this board reviewed them in the case of Attorney General for Canada v. Attorney General for British Columbia and others, and laid down four propositions relative to the legislative competence of Canada and the provinces respectively as established by the decisions of the Judicial committee. These propositions are as follows:-
1.	The legislation of the parliament of the dominion, so long as it strictly relates to subjects of legislation expressly enumerated in section 91 is of paramount authority, even though it trenches upon matters assigned to the provincial legislature by section 02.
Now I am going to venture to make this observation as I go along. Many members will recall the case of the Union Bank and Tennant, a case in which it was contended that the provision made in the Bank Act

by which security may be given without registry by way of chattel mortgage, and that all the power and authority so far as the mortgagee was concerned of a chattel mortgage-that that exercise of power by this parliament was beyond its competence because it infringed on property and civil rights in the province. But the privy council said no; although it does trench upon the exclusive powers of the provincial legislature, nevertheless if it is in its essential character a part of the banking legislation, which is solely within the exclusive legislative jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada, it must prevail, and it did prevail.
The second principle which the Lord Chancellor laid down is this:
2.	The general power of legislation conferred upon the parliament of the dominion by section 91 of the act in supplement of the power to legislate upon the subjects expressly enumerated must be strictly confined to such matters as are unquestionably of national interest and importance, and must not trench on any of the subjects enumerated in section 92, as within the scope of provincial legislation, unless these matters have attained such dimensions as to affect the body politic of the dominion.
3.	It is within the competence of the dominion parliament to provide for matters which though otherwise within the legislative competence of the provincial legislature, are necessarily incidental to effective legislation by the parliament of the dominion upon a subject of legislation expressly enumerated in section 91.
4.	There can be a domain in which provincial and dominion legislation may overlap, in which case, neither legislation will be ultra vires if the field is clear, but if the field is not clear and the two legislations meet, the dominion legislation must prevail.
Those four principles thus stated by the Lord Chancellor are to-day the beacon lights that guide this government in arriving at its conclusions with respect to the subject matter to which I have referred. The application of them is not easy; the reading of them is simple. The ascertainment of the facts to which they apply always becomes more or less complicated, but I think I can submit to this house without difficulty that with respect to hours of labour and with respect to the one day's rest in seven, there is no possible doubt, and especially with respect to the latter having regard to the provisions of the Lord's Day Act as coming within criminal legislation, that we have the authority to legislate.
Now I shall endeavour briefly to indicate how the enunciation of those principles came into being. This country claimed jurisdiction over aviation, complete and absolute. The case was submitted to the Supreme Court of Canada and decided against the contention of the dominion, and the reasons given were 92582-41
those given with respect to the hours of labour, only applied in a different way. It was the opinion of the court, not a unanimous opinion, but it was the opinion of a majority of the court, that aviation in its essential characteristics was engaged in by a government for the purpose of safeguarding its own properties and matters of that sort, and one judge instanced the case of a province initiating a service with that purpose in view. The case ultimately went to the privy council, and in considering that case it became necessary for the Lord Chancellor to make the statement he did. The case was argued before the privy council on the 10th, 14th, 16th, 17th and 20th days of July, 1931, and judgment was given on the 22nd day of October of the same year. I direct attention to the wording. It was those words of the judgment of the Supreme Court of Canada with respect to hours of labour, from which no appeal was taken to the privy council.
I shall trespass on the time of the house to direct attention to the fact that there was outstanding a convention with respect to aeronautics. I will point out that that convention was a convention under this very Peace treaty and that it was a convention that dealt with every phase of aerial navigation. Later parliament did exercise its powers and enact a statute in which regulations were set out at some length, and various other regulations were subsequently made dealing as the lords of the privy council said, with practically every phase of aeronautics. Now bear in mind that section, and I think it is desirable that I should read it at the moment. It is section 132 of our constitution, and section 132 reads as follows:
The parliament and government of Canada-
That is the executive:
-shall have all powers necessary or proper for performing the obligations of Canada or of any province thereof, as part of the British empire, towards foreign countries arising under treaties between the empire and such foreign countries.
It will probably be within the memory of my right hon. friend opposite and the former Minister of Justice that when we were considering the Sockeye Salmon treaty I inquired of the Solicitor General whether he believed we had the power to override provincial rights in a treaty such as that, and I recall his answer. That, of course, was prior to these decisions. I confess that I have doubt, as I believe every member of the profession had, as to just what the decision would be in that set of facts.
Now if hon. gentlemen have followed me up to that point, I think they will realize



International Labour Conventions
that in the aeronautics case we had a treaty between the British empire, Canada being a part of it, and foreign countries, and in that case the privy council decided that section 132 governed and that provincial rights must be subordinate to treaty rights under the provisions of that section. That is the sense of the decision, and as was pointed out by the Lord Chancellor it is very undesirable to attach undue importance to a word or words, but one must always have regard to the ratio decidendi, the sense of the decision itself. Said Lord Chancellor Sankey:
The Supreme Court of Canada has decided the question in its several branches adversely to the claims of the dominion, and has held in effect that while the dominion has a considerable field of jurisdiction in the matter under various heads of section 91 of the British North America Act 1867, there is also a local field of jurisdiction for the provinces, and that the dominion jurisdiction does not extend so far as to permit it to deal with the subject in the broad way in which it has attempted to deal with it in the legislation under consideration.
During the sittings of the Peace Conference in Paris, at the close of the European war, a convention relating to the regulation of aerial navigation, dated the 13th October, 1919, was drawn up by a commission constituted by the Supreme Council of the Peace Conference. That convention was signed by the representatives of the allied and associated powers, including Canada, and was ratified by His Majesty on behalf of the British Empire on the 1st June, 1922. It is now in force between the British Empire and seventeen other states.
With a view to .performing her obligations as part of the British Empire under this convention, which was then in course of preparation, the parliament of Canada enacted the Air Board Act, c. 11, Statutes of Canada 1919 (first session), which, with an amendment thereto, was consolidated in the Revised Statutes of Canada 1927. under the title of the Aeronautics Act, c. 3. It is to be noted, however, that the act does not by reason of its reproduction in the revised statutes take effect as a new law. The governor general in council, on the 31st December, 1919, pursuant to the Air Board Act, issued detailed "Air Regulations" which, with certain amendments, are now in force. _ By the National Defence Act, 1922, the Minister of National Defence thereafter exercised the duties and functions of the air board.
No provincial legislature had enacted any legislation with respect to it but one of them had made protests against the exercise by this parliament of the powers in question. He proceeds:
The determination of these questions depends upon the true construction of sections 91, 92 and 132 of the British North America Act. Section 132 provides as follows:
"The parliament and government of Canada shall have all powers necessary or proper for performing the obligations of Canada or of any province thereof, as part of the British
IMr. Bennett.]
empire, towards foreign countries arising under treaties between the empire and such foreign countries."
It is not necessary to set out at length the familiar sections 91 and 92 which deal with the distribution of legislative powers. Section 91 tabulates the subjects to be dealt with by the dominion, and section 92 the subjects to be dealt with exclusively by the provincial legislatures, but it will not be forgotten that section 91, in addition, authorizes the king by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada to make laws for the peace, order and good government of Canada in relation to all matters not coming within the classes of subjects by this act assigned exclusively to the legislatures of the provinces, and further provides that any matter coming within any of the classes of subjects enumerated in the section shall not be deemed to come within the classes of matters of a local and private nature comprised in the enumeration of classes of subjects assigned by section 92 exclusively to the legislatures of the provinces. The four questions addressed to the court are as follows:
I will not read them except to say that the answers given were to the effect that the dominion and not the provinces had jurisdiction. Now, reading from the Lord Chancellor's judgment:
With regard to sections 91 and 92 the cases which have been decided on the provisions of these sections are legion. Many inquests have been held upon them, and many great lawyers have from time to time dissected them.
Under our system, decided eases effectively construe the words of an act of parliament and established principles and rules whereby its scope and effect may be interpreted. But there is always a danger that in the course of this process the terms of the statute may come to be unduly extended and attention may be diverted from what has been enacted to what has been judicially said about the enactment.
To borrow an analogy; there may be a range of sixty colours, each of which is so little different from its neighbour that it is difficult to make any distinction between the two, and yet at the one end of the range the colour may be white, and at the other end of the range black. Great care must therefore be taken to consider each decision in the light of the circumstances of the case in view of which it was pronounced, especially in the interpretation of an act such as the British North America Act, which was a great constitutional charter, and not to allow general phrases to obscure the underlying object of the act, which was to establish a system of government upon essentially federal principles. Useful as decided cases are, it is always advisable to get back to the words of the act itself and to remember the object with w'hich it was passed...
But while the courts should be jealous in upholding the charter of the provinces as enacted in section 92, it must no less be borne in mind that the real object of the act was to give the central government those high functions and almost sovereign powers by which uniformity of legislation might be secured on all questions which were of common concern to all the provinces as members of a constituent whole.

International Labour Conventions
Upon that observation we base the soundness of this proposed legislation, and these words I cannot too strongly commend to my hon. friends in this chamber:
It must no less be borne in mind that the real object of the act was to give the central government those high functions and almost sovereign powers by which uniformity of legislation might be secured on all questions which were of common concern to all the provinces as members of a constituent whole.
I will not further trespass upon the time of the house with respect to that phase of the judgment, but I will read further these words:
It is therefore obvious that the dominion parliament, in order duly and fully to "perform the obligations of Canada or of any province thereof" under the convention, must make provision for a great variety of subjects. Indeed, the terms of the convention include almost every conceivable matter relating to aerial navigation, and we think that the dominion parliament not only has the right, but also the obligation, to provide by statute and by regulation that the terms of the convention shall be duly carried out. With regard to some of them no doubt it would appear to be clear that the dominion has power to legislate, for example, under section 91, subsection (2), for the regulation of trade and commerce, and under subsection (5), for the postal services, but it is not necessary for the dominion to piece together its powers under section 91 in an endeavour to render them co-extensive with its duty under the convention when section 132 confers upon it full power to do all that is legislatively necessary for the purpose.
Then his lordship summed up in these words:
To sum up, having regard (a) to the terms of section 132; (b) to the terms of the convention which covers almost every conceivable matter relating to aerial navigation; and (c) to the fact that further legislative powers in relation to aerial navigation reside in the parliament of Canada by virtue of section 91, subsections (2), (5), and (7), it would appear that substantially the whole field of legislation in regard to aerial navigation belongs to the dominion. There may be a small portion of the field which is not by virtue of specific words in the British North America Act vested' in the dominion; but neither is it vested by specific words in the provinces. As to such small portion it appears to the board that it must necessarily belong to the dominion under its power to make laws for the peace, order and good government of Canada. Further, their lordships are influenced by the facts that the subject of aerial navigation and the fulfilment of Canadian obligations under section 132 are matters of national interest and importance; and that aerial navigation is a class of subject which has attained' such dimensions as to affect the body politic of the dominion.
That disposes of the aeronautics case, and it will be observed that it is only authority 92582-41J
for one broad proposition. I have read the observations of the Lord Chancellor merely for the purpose of affording some illumination to our minds as we approach the consideration of the problem. The ratio decidendi of the case is that section 132 confers on this parliament the power to discharge every obligation under a treaty, whether it affects the dominion or a province, which we enter into as part of the British empire. It may therefore be taken that wherever, as a part of the empire, a treaty is made by the parliament of Canada, this parliament has complete jurisdiction to deal with every phase of the subject matter of the treaty to the exclusion of the jurisdiction of the provinces of confederation. There remains therefore the second question, which is a more important one: To what extent has this parliament the power, when we have entered into a convention with other countries, to give effect to the terms of that convention when they clash with the jurisdiction which the provinces may have exercised or may exercise? In other words, is the question of the hours of labour per week and the day of rest a question of such importance, and so national in its character, that having bound ourselves thereto we must therefore give effect to it? I have read from the treaty of peace; I have read from the provisions of the League of Nations; I have read from the closing articles of the peace treaty the general provisions with respect to labour, and it will be observed that part of the treaty, which we signed, provides for a forty-eight hour week and for a day of rest. The general provisions are in no doubt at all but in clear-cut positive terms as part of the document which we signed as a part of the British empire, and which deals with that very subject, apart from every other consideration in the world. It deals in exact terms, and I should like to read them. The fourth and fifth guiding principles set down in article 427 of the treaty read:
Fourth-The adoption of an eight hour day or a forty-eight hour week as the standard to be aimed at where it has not already been attained.
Fifth-The adoption of a weekly rest of at least twenty-four hours, which should include Sunday wherever practicable.
Therefore, when the Dominion of Canada emerged from the conclusion of the peace treaty, it had signed it, not on behalf of a province but on behalf of all the citizens of the dominion, a treaty whereby it had bound itself by every means within its power to ensure a forty-eight hour working week and a

International Labour Conventions
day of rest during that period. Can there be any doubt therefore with respect to the jurisdiction of this parliament? Whatever doubts there may have been are fully resolved by the next case to which I direct attention, the radio case which was decided on February 9, 1932. In that case the rights of the provinces were put forward with very great force. It will be recalled that there was a convention outstanding there too. It was not however a convention made by Canada as part of the empire; it was a convention which Canada herself had signed with other countries such as Mexico, United States and Newfoundland. The judgment in that case was delivered by Lord Dunedin who says this-and I am not going to read at great length:
For this must at once he admitted the leading consideration in the judgment of the board

That is in the aeronautics case.
-was that the subject-fell within the provisions of section 132 of the British North America Act.
Which I have already read.
And it is said with truth that, while as regards aviation there was a treaty, the convention here is not a treaty between the empire as such and foreign countries, for Great Britain does not sign as representing the colonies and dominions. She only confirms the assent which had been signified by the colonies and dominions who were separately represented at the meetings which drafted the convention.
Bear in mind that the radio agreement was a convention just as this is. Then he proceeds to say:
But while this is so, the aviation case in their lordships' judgment cannot be put on one side. Counsel for the province felt this and sought to avoid any general deduction by admitting that many of the things provided by the convention and the regulations thereof fell within various special heads of section 91. For example, provisions as to beacon signals he would refer to article 10 of section 91-navigation and shipping. It is unnecessary to multiply instances, because the real point to be considered is this manner of dealing with the subject. In other words, the argument of the province comes to this: Go through all the stipulations of the convention and each one you can pick out which fairly falls within one of the enumerated heads of section 91, that can be held to be appropriate for dominion legislation; but the residue belongs to the province under the head either of article 13 of section 92-property and civil rights, or article 16-matters of a merely local or private nature in the province. Their lordships cannot agree that the matter should be so dealt with. Canada as a dominion is one of the signatories to the convention. In a question with foreign powers the persons who might infringe some of the stipulations in the convention would not be the Dominion of Canada as a whole but would be [Mr. Bcnaett.J
individual persons residing in Canada. These persons must, so to speak, be kept in order by legislation and the only legislation that can deal with them all at once is dominion legislation. This idea of Canada as a dominion being bound by a convention equivalent to a treaty with foreign powers was quite unthought of in 1867. It is the outcome of the gradual development of the position of Canada vis-a-vis to the mother country Great Britain, which is found in these later days expressed in the Statute of Westminster. It is not therefore to be expected that such a matter should be dealt with in explicit words in either section 91 or section 92. The only class of treaty which would bind Canada was thought of as a treaty by Great Britain, and that was provided for by section 132. Being, therefore, not mentioned explicitly in either section 91 or section 92, such legislation falls within the general words at the opening of section 91 which assigned to the government of the dominion the power to make laws "for the peace, order and good government of Canada in relation to all matters not coming within the classes of subjects by this act assigned exclusively to the legislatures of the provinces." In fine, though agreeing that the convention was not such a treaty as is defined in section 132, their lordships think that it comes to the same thing. On the 11th August, 1927, the Privy Council of Canada, with the approval of the Governor General, chose a body to attend the meeting of all the powers to settle international agreements as to wireless. The Canadian body attended and took part in deliberations. The deliberations ended in the convention with general regulations appended being signed at Washington on the 25th November, 1927, by the representatives of all the powers who had taken part in the conference, and this convention was ratified by the Canadian government on the 12th July, 1928. The result is in their lordships' opinion clear. It is Canada as a whole which is amenable to the other powers for the proper carrying out of the convention; and to prevent individuals in Canada infringing the stipulations of the convention it is necessary that the dominion should pass legislation which should apply to all the dwellers in Canada.
I will not detain the house by reading further from the judgment; that is sufficient for my purposes.
There is one word more I desire to say as to an additional ground upon which the proposed legislation is supported. It will be recalled that in dealing with the case of a federal union the treaty provides for a discretion being exercised. I particularly dwelt upon that provision. The discretion might be exercised by sending the recommendation down to a province and it might be exercised as we now propose to exercise it, by legislation in this house. That discretion which is vested in the government of Canada was exercised, it is true, in one way at one time. We now propose to exercise it as indicated in the judgments in the radio and aeronautics

International Labour Conventions
cases. We propose to exercise it as a matter that affects the whole of Canada in which uniform legislation with respect to hours of labour is a question not only of national interest; we cannot go behind the words of the covenant of the League of Nations which declares it to be of international concern. It is not provincial, not national, but international. Under these circumstances, how otherwise can we seriously become a party to a treaty that declares the matter with which we now propose to deal is one of interest not only to us as a nation but to other nations as well because it concerns the well-being and happiness of all nations and does something to secure and make for universal peace? It is on that principle that we support the legislation. Without going into the matter at any greater length-and I apologize to the house for trespassing so long upon its attention with respect to a matter of such vital importance-I move that we approve this convention on the basis of which we are founding the legislation, notice of which is now standing in my name.

speechtext:
I must say
that I envy my right hon. friend's fine power of confidence in his own views, and I should like to be as sure as he is of any opinion I may offer on a question of this kind. However, I humbly beg to differ from the views he has expressed and to say that his preliminary words to the effect that the government has resolved this question of jurisdiction are a little too hopeful. I am afraid that whatever the action of parliament on the proposed draft convention may be, nothing will be changed as to the respective jurisdictions of the provinces and the federal parliament.
May I say at the outset that I am one of those who believe in the principle of an eight hour day and a forty-eight hour week. I believe in many fields of activity the week might be even shorter, and I shall not surprise my right hon. friend when I say that conditions to-day as to an eight hour day and a forty-eight hour week are quite different from what they were when this draft convention was adopted at Washington. At that time this was the goal which labour wanted to reach, but that is not so to-day; and at the last international labour conference there was submitted a new draft convention making it a forty hour week of labour. All the representatives of labour at the convention strongly urged the adoption of that draft convention. Some of the employers objected and most of the governments' representatives were absent
when the final vote was taken. I am sorry to say that the Canadian representative was one of them. I shall quote his words later. He gave as an excuse that in Canada this power belongs to the provinces. At that time he had not been acquainted with the change of view of the law officers of the crown and probably of my right hon. friend. I say that by way of pointing out that no tremendously radical change is involved, because the provisions of this convention are as a matter of fact now in force in most of the provinces of Canada, and in most of the occupations of the Canadian people.
My right hon. friend bases his contention as to the jurisdiction of this parliament on article 23 of the peace treaty, and on the various sections of the labour part of that treaty. Section 23 reads as follows-and it is very important to note the first two lines:
Subject to and in accordance with the provisions of international conventions existing or hereafter to be agreed upon,-
The whole section is qualified by those two lines, "subject to and in accordance with the provisions of international conventions existing or hereafter to be agreed upon."

speechtext: International conventions.

maintopic: EIGHT HOUR DAY AND FORTY-EIGHT HOUR WEEK IN INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext:
What are those conventions which are to be agreed upon? They are defined, the labour part, as the Prime Minister has said, in the labour part of the peace treaty, which provides in the main for two things: first, the organization of international labour machinery, known as the international labour office, and second, an international labour conference, that being the meeting which takes place annually or twice a year of the representatives of all the countries which are members of the League of Nations; and of late some countries which are not members of the league have joined the international labour office, I am very pleased to say, for the purpose of discussing and coming to decisions on subjects of interest to labour. How is it done? Article 405 of the treaty states how it is done:
When the conference has decided on the adoption of proposals with regard to an item in the agenda, it will rest with the conference to determine whether these proposals shall take the form:	(a) of a recommendation to be
submitted to the members for consideration with a view to effect being given to it by national legislation or otherwise, or (b) of a draft international convention for ratification by the members.
It is provided that a majority of two-thirds of the votes cast by the delegates present shall be necessary, and so forth; and that the con-

International Labour Conventions
ferenee shall have due regard to those countries in which climatic conditions, the imperfect development of industrial organization or other special circumstances prevail. Then it is said in the same article:
Each of the members undertakes that it will, within the period of one year at most from the closing of the session of the conference, or if it is impossible owing to exceptional circumstances to do so within the period of one year, then at the earliest practicable moment and in no case later than eighteen months from the closing of the session of the conference, bring the recommendation or draft convention before the authority or authorities within whose competence the matter lies, for the enactment of legislation or other action.
In the case of a recommendation, the members will inform the Secretary-General of the action taken.
In the case of a draft convention, the member will, if it obtains the consent of the authority or authorities within whose competence the matter lies-*
I draw particular attention to those words:
-communicate the formal ratification of the convention to the Secretary-General and will take such action as may be necessary to make effective the provisions of such convention.
If on a recommendation no legislative or other action is taken to make a recommendation effective, or if the draft convention fails to obtain the consent of the authority or authorities within whose competence the matter lies-
And again I draw the attention of the house to those words:
-no further obligation shall rest upon the member.
In the case of a federal state, the power of which to enter into conventions on labour matters is subject to limitations, it shall be in the discretion of that government to treat a draft convention to which such limitations apply as a recommendation only, and the provisions of this article with respect to recommendations shall apply in such case.
These are the only forms of procedure devised for the international labour conference in the exercise of the functions entrusted to it by the peace treaty for the purpose of dealing with labour matters as they affect the nations of the world. As I have stated, Canada in the case of a draft convention will approve if it obtains the consent of the authority or authorities within whose competence the matter lies; the framers of the treaty quite realizing that there are countries in which there would be different jurisdictions as to the matters with which the draft conventions might deal, and that the member, in this case Canada, has first to obtain the consent of the authority or authorities within whose competence the matter lies. And it is further stated that if the draft convention fails to obtain the consent of the authority or
fMr. Lapointe.]
authorities within whose competence the matter lies, no further obligation will rest upon the member.
Well, what were the duties of Canada? My right hon. friend puts reliance on section 132 of the British North America Act in his argument that this comes within the power and jurisdiction of the federal parliament. Section 132 states:
The parliament and government of Canada shall have all powers necessary or proper for performing the obligations of Canada or of any province thereof, as part of the British empire, towards foreign countries arising under such treaties between the empire and such foreign countries.
Under section 132 it is the obligation that creates the jurisdiction. If there is no obligation on the part of the government or parliament, and I claim that under the sections of the peace treaty which I have read there is no such obligation, then section 132 fails to give jurisdiction to this parliament because there is not that obligation which alone creates the jurisdiction.
How did Canada act in this matter? My right hon. friend claims that all has been changed as a result of the judgments in the radio and aviation cases, with which I will deal later. Wfiat did Canada do? The views of this country were expressed by the government in an order in council dated November 6, 1920, and I wish to put part of this order in council once more on Hansard. It is P.C. 2722, and was based on the report of the then Minister of Justice. It reads as follows:
The minister further states that he is of opinion that the provisions of the labour part of the Treaty of I ersailles do not impose any obligation on the Dominion of Canada to enact into law the different draft conventions or recommendations which may from time to time be adopted by the conference. The obligation as set forth is simply in the nature of an undertaking on the part of each member within the period of one year at most from the closing of the session of the conference, or if it is impossible owing to exceptional circumstances to do so within a period of one year, then at the earliest practicable moment, and in any case not later than eighteen months from the closing of the conference "to bring the recommendations or draft conventions before the authority or authorities within whose competence the matter lies for the enactment of legislation or other action." The treaty engagement being of this character, it is not such as to justify legislation on the part of parliament under the authority of section 132 of the British North America Act, 1867, to give effect to any of the proposals of the said draft conventions and recommendations, which must be held, as between the dominion and the provinces, to be within the legislative competence of the latter. The government's obligation will, in the opinion of tlie minister, be fully carried out if the

International Labour Conventions
After Recess
different conventions and recommendations are brought before the competent authority, dominion or provincial, accordingly as it may appear, having regard to the scope and objects, the true nature and character of the legislation required to give effect to the proposals of the conventions and recommendations respectively, that they fall within the legislative competence of the one or the other.
That order in Council also embodied the minister's opinion on the very question whether the provisions of the draft convention limiting hours of work in industrial undertakings to eight in the day and forty-eight in the week, adopted at the first session of the international labour conference at Washington, came within the legislative competence of the parliament of Canada or of the provincial legislatures. In the same order in council the minister reported that the proposals of this convention-and these are the words of the Minister of Justice, as contained in the order in council:
-involve legislation which is competent to parliament in so far as dominion works and undertakings are affected, but which the provincial legislatures have otherwise the power to enact and apply generally and comprehensively.
In 1923 there was a dominion-provincial conference, which I attended together with the then Minister of Labour. All these draft conventions were submitted to the delegates to that conference, and all agreed that these were matters for provincial action. In 1924 the then Prime Minister, my right hon. leader, moved a resolution which was adopted by the house, and which will be found at page 2466 of Hansard for May 23, 1924. The resolution read:
Resolved that it is expedient that a certain draft convention which was adopted at the first session of the international labour conference of the League of Nations, in 1919, limiting the hours of work in industrial undertakings to eight in the day and forty-eight in the week, be referred to the select committee on industrial and international relations for examination and report, having regard to the labour provisions of the treaties of peace and to the order in council of November 0, 1920, dealing with the jurisdiction of the dominion parliament and the provincial legislatures.
That committee, of which the Minister of Justice and I were members, sat and reported to the house that in spite of the order in council of 1920 and the views expressed by the law officers, the matter was of such importance that it should be submitted to the Supreme Court of Canada by way of a reference.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, when the
house rose at six o'clock I was proceeding to indicate what Canada has done regarding the draft convention in connection with the eight hour day. I forgot to mention that from September 5 to September 7, 1922, a dominion-provincial conference was held in Ottawa as a result of which the following resolution was adopted:
That the conference has had under consideration the various proposals relative to labour which have emanated during the past three years from the international labour conference of the League of Nations. It is provided under the treaties of peace that the draft conventions and recommendations of this body must be brought to the attention of the authority or authorities within whose competence the matter lies for the enactment of legislation or other action, and this conference is of the view that the authorities deemed to be respectively competent to deal with the matters in question should give careful and sympathetic attention to such draft conventions and recommendations with a view to enacting necessary legislation where this may be found practicable, and that the federal government undertakes on request from a majority of provincial governments to call a conference for the consideration of any aspects of these matters when this may be deemed necessary.
It was to give effect to this recommendation that the federal-provincial conference to which I referred this afternoon was called in
1923.	I quoted the motion made on May 23, 1924 by the then Prime Minister, the present leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) referring this draft convention limiting the hours otf work in industrial undertakings to the industrial and international relations committee.
That committee in turn reported to the house that although various opinions had been given it believed in order to obtain a final decision the matter should be referred to the Supreme Court of Canada. When the report came before the house for discussion the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) took part in the debate. Speaking on July 18,
1924,	on an amendment moved by the present hon member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) the Minister of Justice is reported as having said the following:
I do not think there is any doubt as to the jurisdiction of this parliament in regard to dominion labour. But there is more than a doubt in regard to our jurisdiction to apply the eight hour day principle generally throughout the dominion. I have not a doubt upon the subject; I am satisfied that the ruling of the Department of Justice is right in that respect, and that the provincial legislatures have jurisdiction in such matters; but I run

International Labour Conventions
just as sure that this parliament has jurisdiction in regard to dominion works, and if parliament or the government is in sympathy with the proposal of the eight hour day as applicable to dominion operations and dominion works, there is no reason why this proposal should not be supported.
Then he added:
I would not support the amendment if it proposed to extend that principle into provincial jurisdictions over which I am satisfied we have no control. But a6 the amendment is purely applicable to dominion works I think it is in the right direction and I shall support it.
I commend to the present Minister of Justice the opinion held in 1924 by Hon. Hugh Guthrie.
