speechtext:
We will see about that later. In the same debate the then leader of the opposition, Right Hon. Arthur Meighen, a former prime minister of Canada, who had much to do with the League of Nations and the international labour office, who is a distinguished jurist and who was never very anxious to make things easy for the then government, used the following language as reported at page 4763 of Hansard:
But I really think the question of jurisdiction is very well determined. I would have been content to accept the Justice department's view as to where our jurisdiction ends and where that of the provinces commences. I have my own opinions and I do not know that they differ from those of others on this subject. However, if there is something still in doubt, if particularly the Justice department has doubt, I have no objection to the submission to the supreme court. But the submission itself is not reailly any progress. It cannot be stated that by the submission we are taking any very effective step to carry out our undertaking.
Air. Martel: May I ask my right hon. friend a question, not for the purpose of interrupting him, but as a lawyer? Where does he think the power rests to enact an eight hour day, in the provinces or in the federal authorities?
Air. Aleighen:	It rests certainly with the
federal authorities so far as federal works are concerned. I do not know myself of any sphere where else it rests. I think the rest of the spheres are the provinces, and I never knew there was any real question of doubt in the matter. But there may be some clause as to which there is doubt, and if the Justice department so holds, the submission is right, but if the submission is merely for the purpose of delay, it is wrong.

Further on at pages 4764 and 4765 Mr. Meighen said:
We have no right in the world to invade jurisdiction where provincial jurisdiction is clear, and do so under the guise of declaring this work or that for the general advantage of Canada. To do so would be the grossest abuse of the powers of this house, and I would not for one moment consider any such suggestion, no matter from what side of the house it emanated. This expresses my general idea of a most embarrassing question, and I give it, not in any spirit of criticism, but merely as' my understanding of what this country is pledged to under the Geneva convention

Mark these words:
-and as well of what we are pledged to keep away from under our obligations as a party to the contract of confederation.
Reference was then made to the Supreme Court of Canada. The dominion government was represented before the supreme court by the present Deputy Minister of Justice as solicitor and by the late Eugene Lafleur, a distinguished jurist of Montreal, and Mr. O'Donoghue of Toronto as counsel for the attorney general of Canada. I wish to quote a few words from the factum presented to the supreme court, signed by Mr. Lafleur and his associate counsel, speaking on behalf of the justice department and for himself as a distinguished jurist. Having quoted article 405 of the peace treaty, which has been recited in this house this afternoon two or three times, he said:
It is obvious that these provisions of the labour part of the treaty do not impose any obligation on the dominion to enact into law tile different draft conventions or recommendations which may from time to time be adopted by the conference. This is merely an undertaking on the part of each member to bring the recommendations or draft conventions before the proper authorities.
This being the extent of the obligation, it does not justify legislation on the part of parliament to give effect to any such recommendations or draft conventions under the authority of section 132 of the British North America Act, which provides that the parliament and government of Canada shall have all powers necessary or proper for performing the obligations of Canada or of any province thereof, as part of the British Empire, towards foreign countries arising out of treaties between the empire and such foreign countries. The government's obligation will be satisfied if the different recommendations or conventions are brought before the competent authority, dominion or provincial, as the case may be.
And he adds:
The legislatures of the provinces are the authorities within whose competence the subject-matter of the draft convention lies and before whom such draft convention should be brought under the provisions of article 405 of the treaty of peace, for the enactment of legislation or any other action that may be deemed

International Labour Conventions
proper. This, it is submitted, is the case, subject to the sole exception of the legislation respecting dominion works and undertakings, as will be explained in answer to question 4.
The subject-matter is evidently included in items 13 and 16 of section 92 of the British North America Act, inasmuch as the regulation of the hours of labour affects civil rights in the province and if confined to labour performed in a province would be a matter of merely local or private nature in the province.
This being so, the legislative jurisdiction of the province over the subject-matter must be exclusive and would not be overborne by any attempt on the part of the dominion parliament to legislate for the peace, order and good government of Canada, conferred by the first part of section 91, inasmuch as that power is only given in relation to matters not coming within the classes of subjects by the act assigned exclusively to the legislatures of the provinces. This point has been dealt with several times by the privy council, and it is only necessary to refer to the observations of Lord Haldane in the most recent case of Toronto Electric Commissioners versus Snider 1925, A.C., at pages 410-413.
As my right hon. friend is relying for the jurisdiction of this parliament, apart from article 23 and the labour part of the peace treaty, upon the residue power for peace, order and good government contained in section 91, I think it proper that I should read what section 91 says. The part of section 91 which concerns this matter reads as follows:
It shall be lawful for the Queen, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons, to make laws for the peace, order and good government of Canada, in relation to all matters not coming within the classes of subjects by this act assigned exclusively to the legislatures of the provinces.
As was stated by the privy council in the case of Snider of Toronto, this question of hours of labour is exclusively assigned to the legislatures by section 92, and cannot come under this part of section 91 regarding the residue of matters which may be dealt with by this parliament for peace, order and good government.
Now I come to the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada on the reference which was submitted to the court and to which my right hon. friend alluded this afternoon. It will be found in the Supreme court reports of 1925, page 505. I shall quote only the answer to the last question, because that is the one with which we are mainly concerned, dealing with the possible jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada in the matter. The question was:
If the subject-matter of the said draft convention be. in part only, within the competence of the legislatures of the provinces, then in what particular or particulars, or to what
extent, is the subject-matter of the draft convention within the competence of the parliament of Canada?
To that fourth question the supreme court answered as follows:
The parliament of Canada has exclusive legislative authority in those parts of Canada not within the boundaries of any province, and also upon the subjects dealt with in the draft convention in relation to the servants of the dominion government.
That is the jurisdiction of Canada in the matter of hours of labour. Then how can section 132 of the British North America Act apply? If there is no obligation, as was stated this afternoon, on the part of Canada with regard to this convention, where is our jurisdiction? It is the obligation towards foreign powers which gives to parliament jurisdiction to deal with a matter of this kind when bound by treaty so to do. Where are we bound? Well, it is only necessary to read section 405 of the peace treaty to find out what obligation, if any, there is on the part of this parliament or of the dominion with regard to a draft convention. It is not even called a convention; it is a draft convention, or in French, un projet de convention. There is nothing final to it. It is something which is suggested to the various members of this international labour conference for the purpose of their calling it to the attention of the authority within whose competence the matter lies to take any action regarding it which they see fit. Even the competent authority is not bound in any way. It is only a draft convention, I repeat. Then how can it be said to constitute an obligation on the part of Canada giving to this parliament under section 132 of the British North America Act authority and jurisdiction to deal with the matter? It is clear that the countries are not bound by it. Over fifty nations are members of the international labour organization. I do not think there are seventeen at the present time which have approved or ratified that draft convention, and my hon. friend claims that it is an obligation binding upon Canada. Well, let us proceed.
We were bound, so far as the employees of the dominion are concerned, by the decision of the supreme court, and it had also always been the view of the law officers of the crown in that respect. And to give effect to this obligation P.C. 670, an order in council approved by the governor general on March 27, 1930, was laid on the table of the house on March 31, as you will find at page 1082-3 of Hansard. By this order in council the dominion extended to all employees of the

International Labour Conventions
government of Canada the principle of the forty-eight hour week and of eight hours a day, and all the obligations by which Canada was bound were complied with when this order in council was passed by the government.
Under this administration-and this I wish to call particularly to the attention of the Minister of Justice-on February 17, 1932, at page 284 of Hansard, the then member for Kenora-Rainy River, Mr. Heenan, moved the following resolution:
Whereas, the Dominion of Canada is a signatory to the articles of peace of the treaties of Versailles, thereby subscribing to the principle of a maximum working day of eight hours: Therefore be it resolved that this house is of opinion that the government of Canada should take appropriate steps to ensure, throughout Canada, the fulfilment of our treaty obligations and conventions arising out of the peace treaty, relating to hours of work.
Mr. Heenan did not claim in his speech that this parliament had jurisdiction over the matter. He said:
In 1930, in order to carry out our treaty obligations, an order in council was passed, P.C. 670, putting all federal government employees who were working in excess of eight hours on an eight-hour day basis. On May 30 of the same year legislation was enacted, now known as chapter 20-21 of George V. placing all employees on government contracts or working at day labour on government work on the eight-hour day basis. My position in the matter is simply this. Mr. Speaker. 1 submit that the federal parliament having taken the mote out of its own eye, the federal government is now in a better position to approach the provincial governments with a view to having them enact legislation to carry out our treaty obligations. It will be seen, therefore, that this resolution simply calls upon the government of Canada to take appropriate steps to ensure throughout Canada the fulfilment of our treaty obligations with respect to hours of work. And I have no fear but that this house will unanimously adopt the resolution.
The Minister of Justice spoke for the government, as reported at page 286 of Hansard of the same day. He said:
The gist of the motion is that the government should take appropriate steps. As the motion was not carried during the last session of the house there were no steps to be taken, as a result of it. In fact the only steps that suggest themselves to my mind at the moment are those which were taken by the preceding government on four or five occasions, when the question was brought to the attention of the various provincial governments with the idea of enlisting their sympathies and having them pass the necessary provincial legislation to bring into force the provisions of the treaty of Versailles with respect to labour.

In my judgment this parliament has done about all it can do in respect of that treaty. The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River has given a brief resume of some of the steps which have been taken by this parliament to bring our national labour service into conformity with the requirements of that treaty, but fortunately or unfortunately the dominion powers are limited by our constitutional act; there are some matters which do not lie within our legislative jurisdiction and in connection with which we have no right whatever to legislate. One of these matters is the question of hours of labour, which is largely a provincial matter, and the most this government can do in regard to the general subject is to bring that question directly to the attention of the various provincial governments and request them to cooperate.
This has been done time and time again. It was not done directly after last session because the motion was not adopted by the house last session, but if this present motion is adopted the government will take steps without delay definitely to draw this matter to the attention of the various provincial governments.
Further on, the Minister of Justice made these observations, which I commend to the Prime Minister, who this afternoon took the view that Canada had not fulfilled most of its duties with regard to these conventions:
There is this further to be said in regard to Canada and the treaty of Versailles, and particularly with respect to the question of labour. While in Geneva last fall I had occasion to discuss the question with some of those who are better informed in regard to these matters than I am myself, and I was glad to learn that Canada was not lagging behind in regard to the provisions of that treaty. We were well in the forefront. I do not think any nation in the world has carried out all the provisions of that treaty. Some have done so to a much greater extent than others, but Canada's position is a very happy one in that respect. We have gone a much greater distance than many other nations perhaps more important in one aspect than Canada, and I felt very proud of the work that this dominion had accomplished.
My hon. friend said that his former opinions were expressed before the decision of the privy council was given. Well, the decision of the privy council in the aviation case, which is the one upon which my right hon. friend bases his argument-my right hon. friend shakes his head-

I said that the purport
of the aviation decision was that section 132 governed. The radio case went further.

maintopic: EIGHT HOUR DAY AND FORTY-EIGHT HOUR WEEK IN INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKINGS

Would it surprise my
right hon. friend to know that the radio case had been decided at the time?

speechtext:
When the Minister of
Justice said that, yes.

speechtext: The Minister of Justice spoke, as I have quoted his words, on February 17, 1932.

speechtext: The decision was February 9.

maintopic: EIGHT HOUR DAY AND FORTY-EIGHT HOUR WEEK IN INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext:
The decision in the
aviation case had been delivered by the privy council on October 22, 1931, a few months before, and the radio decision had been delivered on February 9, 1932. Both those judgments were rendered before my right hon. friend expressed his opinion as he did.
I have something which is even better than that. Even the right hon. gentleman took a long time to change his views after the decisions in the aviation and the radio cases. One of those decisions was given in 1931 and the other in February, 1932. Only a few months ago, when my right hon. friend left for Europe, he sent to all the provincial premiers a letter dated August 31, 1934, and that letter was made public by the then Acting Prime Minister, the hon. member for Argenteuil (Sir George Perley) on September 13 last. It was published in all the newspapers of Canada on September 14 last. What was the view of my right hon. friend at that time? He says now that the question of jurisdiction has been resolved in favour of this parliament. It was not resolved in September last, because my right hon. friend in his letter, having said that it was his purpose to call a conference of the provincial premiers when he returned from the old country, stated that he wanted to place upon the agenda certain matters, one of them being the following-it was second on the list:
Are the provinces prepared to surrender their exclusive jurisdiction over legislation dealing with such social problems as old age pensions, unemployment and social insurance, hours and conditions for work, minimum wages, et cetera, to the dominion parliament? If so, on what terms and conditions?	[DOT]

maintopic: EIGHT HOUR DAY AND FORTY-EIGHT HOUR WEEK IN INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext: That was their stand.

maintopic: EIGHT HOUR DAY AND FORTY-EIGHT HOUR WEEK IN INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext:
Am I not right when I say that when my right hon. friend wrote that letter to the provincial premiers on August 31, 1934, he had not reached the conclusion that we could simply say: We have the power, the jurisdiction, and we are going to exercise it? He was then of the opinion that this was the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces. If it was the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces in September, 1934, it is just as much so in February, 1935, and it was so when my right hon. friend spoke over the air in January of this year. Those broadcast expressions of my right hon. friend, fine as
they were, never had the effect of changing the constitution of Canada. They have not changed the constitution; the matter is still a provincial one, and if labour relies on the government's attitude for a new deal, I am afraid it will be a misdeal, because the proposed legislation will not have the validity which any parliamentary action concerning a matter so important should have.
My right hon. friend relies on the two decisions in regard to radio and aviation. Let me' say first that the question of provincial jurisdiction in matters such as this has been decided by the privy council many times in such cases as the Board of Commerce Act, the fair prices act of 1929; Toronto Electric Commissioners and Snider in 1925, where the question of peace, order and good government was dealt with by the privy council. My right hon. friend says that there has been a change; that there had been a development going on with regard to our respective powers, our respective jurisdiction. Well, even at that time the question was discussed and debated with regard to aviation and radio, and the privy council delivered judgment confirming provincial jurisdiction in various matters. They did it in the fisheries case in 1929, with which the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) is well acquainted. They did it in connection with the Insurance Act in 1932, and I think the case is reported in the same volume of the appeal cases or the Dominion Law Reports where they decided in favour of the provinces. The only matter on which they based their decision was section 132 in both the aviation case and the radio case, but in both those cases there was no draft convention; there was a binding treaty on which the privy council based its decision. In regard to aerial navigation the treaty had been signed in 1920 with a large number of foreign powers, and my right hon. friend has read part of the judgment of the privy council. I desire to read a few words of it also as recorded on page 58:
Their lordships do not think that aeronautics is a class of subject within property and civil rights in the provinces, although hereagain. ingenious arguments may show that some small part of it might be so included.
Surely that cannot be said about hours of work.
Their lordships are of opinion that it is proper to take a broader view of the matter rather than to rely on forced analogies or piecemeal analysis. They consider the governing section to be section 132, which gives to the parliament and government of Canada all powers necessary and proper for performing the obligations towards foreign countries arising
International Labour Conventions

under treaties between the empire and such foreign countries. As far as section 132 is concerned, their lordships are not aware of any decided case which is of assistance on the present occasion. It will be observed, however, from the very definite words of the section, that it is the parliament and government of Canada who are to have all powers necessary or proper for performing the obligations of Canada or any province thereof.
To sum up, having regard (a) to the terms of section 132; (b) to the terms of the convention which covers almost every conceivable matter relating to aerial navigation; and (c) to the fact that further legislative powers in relation to aerial navigation reside in the parliament of Canada by virtue of section 91 (2), (5) and (7), it would appear that substantially the whole field of legislation in regard to aerial navigation belongs to the dominion. There may be a small portion of the field which is not by virtue of specific words in the British North America Act vested in the dominion; but neither is it vested by specific words in the provinces. As to such small portion it appears to the board that it must necessarily belong to the dominion under its power to make laws for the peace, order and good government of Canada. Further their lordships are influenced by the facts that the subjects^ of aerial navigation and the fulfilment of Canadian obligations under section 132 are matters of national interest and importance; and that aerial navigation is a class of subject which has attained such dimensions as to affect the body politic of the dominion.
The decision in the radio case was given a few months afterwards, on February 9, 1932. There again it was to confirm a treaty; that is to say the legislation that was passed was passed in consequence of a treaty binding Canada, signed at Washington on November 25, 1927 by the representatives of all the powers which had taken part in the conference; and this convention was ratified by the Canadian government on July 12, 192S.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: EIGHT HOUR DAY AND FORTY-EIGHT HOUR WEEK IN INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext: It was a convention, not a treaty.

maintopic: EIGHT HOUR DAY AND FORTY-EIGHT HOUR WEEK IN INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext:
It was a convention signed and binding and ratified, not a draft convention. There were, I think, eighteen obligations in the treaty which Canada had to fulfil. The idea pervading that judgment is that the whole subject of aeronautics is so completely covered by the treaty ratified between the nations that there is not enough left to give a separate field to the provinces as regards that subject. But let me say this: the law officers of the crown, while they were giving their opinion that the hours of work were under provincial jurisdiction, and never had any doubt in the matter, always claimed that radio and aviation were federal matters.

They always made a clear distinction as between these two matters and matters which come so clearly under property and civil rights, one of the classes of subjects which are exclusively provincial.
I said this afternoon that this question of the forty-eight hour week is not such a burning question at the present time. It was such a question in 1919, but almost everywhere the forty-eight hour week of labour has been adopted. Canadian labour, as well as labour in the other countries, is no longer claiming the forty-eight hour week; they are asking for forty hours.

maintopic: EIGHT HOUR DAY AND FORTY-EIGHT HOUR WEEK IN INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext: No, thirty hours.

maintopic: EIGHT HOUR DAY AND FORTY-EIGHT HOUR WEEK IN INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext:
Well, I did not think my hon. friend was going as far as that. But I know that all the representatives of labour at the last international labour conference in Geneva insisted on a new draft convention of forty hours a week. And the draft convention had been prepared. There had even been a preliminary conference about it, called the tri-partite conference, I think, in 1933, which had made a very interesting report on the matter and which had drafted a projected convention to be adopted by the international conference which was to take place last year. The draft convention was adopted in the committee, but when it came before the whole conference most of the delegates of the governments mysteriously disappeared; they were not there to vote, and although the draft convention carried by a pretty good majority there was not a sufficient quorum under the rules of the international labour conference to give validity to it. I was interested in reading in the record of the proceedings of that conference of 1934, on page 338, the remarks of Canada's delegate, who had been one of those absent when the vote was taken. There was a demand for an adjournment, and Doctor Riddell said:
I rise to support the proposal of Mr. Martens for an adjournment. In connection with his statement, I might be permitted a word in explanation of our vote on article 1. The government of Canada is a federal government. The Supreme Court of Canada has declared that the question of hours is a provincial matter. The provinces have stated in their replies to the questionnaire that the office draft did not offer sufficient flexibility for them to aprove of the adoption of that draft. The amended draft went still further; therefore we had no option but to abstain.
So even the representatives of Canada, speaking for Canada at the international labour conference, were giving as a reason

International Labour Conventions
for their line of action at the last international labour conference the fact that under the constitution of Canada hours of work are a matter of provincial jurisdiction.

maintopic: EIGHT HOUR DAY AND FORTY-EIGHT HOUR WEEK IN INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext:
If I may ask a question,
who was the representative who took that stand at the Geneva conference?

maintopic: EIGHT HOUR DAY AND FORTY-EIGHT HOUR WEEK IN INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext: Doctor Riddell.

maintopic: EIGHT HOUR DAY AND FORTY-EIGHT HOUR WEEK IN INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext: He was a government representative?

maintopic: EIGHT HOUR DAY AND FORTY-EIGHT HOUR WEEK IN INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext: Yes.

speechtext:
Acting under government
instructions?

maintopic: EIGHT HOUR DAY AND FORTY-EIGHT HOUR WEEK IN INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext: I suppose so.

maintopic: EIGHT HOUR DAY AND FORTY-EIGHT HOUR WEEK IN INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext: No, he is the permanent representative at Geneva. He was not instructed.

maintopic: EIGHT HOUR DAY AND FORTY-EIGHT HOUR WEEK IN INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext:
I have been a delegate
of Canada to various conferences at Geneva, both constitutional and as to labour matters, and as a delegate I would not have taken a stand like this without first asking for instructions from the government I represented; that is all I can say.
Now I was saying that this forty hour week of labour is not a very radical thing at the present time. I have heard it said occasion-all that my own province of Quebec is sometimes backward in matters of labour legislation. That of course is not correct; for Quebec has led in many respects with regard to labour legislation. But may I call the attention of the house to an act respecting the limiting of working hours, passed by the Quebec legislature in 1933, 23 George V, chapter 40, which gives to the lieutenant governor in council the right to order the number of hours per week or per day during which a workman employed in manual labour may work; and in no case should the number of working hours be less than six per day or thirty-three per week, so that as far as possible employment might be assured for two or more crews of workmen employed at the same work. There have been proclamations under this act. On July 14, 1933, the building industry, comprising the building, repairing and demolishing of buildings of every kind, and covering especially the men employed as bricklayers, carpenters, joiners, cement finishers, roofers and so on, were all brought under this act. From and after July 1, 1933, the duration of effective labour in the building industry within the limits of the Montreal division should not exceed eight hours per day and the total hours of effective labour
in the course of a single week should not in any case exceed forty, eight hours less than is proposed under this draft convention. Other trades and occupations since have been brought under the operations of that law, so this is not such a great discovery.

maintopic: EIGHT HOUR DAY AND FORTY-EIGHT HOUR WEEK IN INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext: That has not been applied to the textile industry?

maintopic: EIGHT HOUR DAY AND FORTY-EIGHT HOUR WEEK IN INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext:
I do not think so, but it should be. I am quite willing to agree with my hon. friend in that regard, and to say that it should apply to the textile industry as well
I have spoken at greater length than I had intended, Mr. Speaker, and I do not know that I have anything to add except this: Mj hon. friend from East Hamilton (Mr. Mitchell), who is a good friend of mine, became very enthusiastic this afternoon over this great change, with the parliament of the dominion assuming jurisdiction with regard to draft conventions of the international labour conference. The other day I heard my hon. friend from North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) express himself as being very much pleased, when the resolution in connection with unemployment insurance was under discussion, because at last the parliament of Canada was assuming jurisdiction in the matter. May I tell my hon. friends that the assumption of jurisdiction does not create it. I believe they respect the constitution as much as I do, and may I tell them that the safeguards and protections in the constitution are more important to the labour people than they are to those who employ them. The safeguards in the constitution are more important to the minorities than they are to the majorities. They are more important to the poor than to the wealthy, because the wealthy always find a way to protect themselves. So when there is such an obvious encroachment as this on the powers of the provinces under the constitution I say that my hon. friends may be ill advised to be pleased that parliament should go beyond and over the constitution. I think those who have at heart the progress of labour legislation, those who want reforms as much as my right hon. friend does, will think it better to achieve those reforms in a valid way. There should be no loopholes left. No one will receive anything if labour is given not an instrument which is legal and valid, but something which is against the constitution and which will not stand in our courts.
I see that my right hon. friend has given notice of a bill to enforce this provision. I sincerely hope that before this bill becomes part of the statutes of Canada the jurisdiction of this parliament will be ascertained, or at

International Labour Conventions
least that there will be some understanding and agreement with the provinces, whom my right hon. friend wanted to meet last September because of their exclusive jurisdiction in the matter, so that good and valid legislation may be placed on the statute books of Canada regarding hours of labour and other progressive labour legislation, which I am quite willing to support.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: EIGHT HOUR DAY AND FORTY-EIGHT HOUR WEEK IN INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think in all parts of
the house there will be absolute agreement that since the two decisions of the judicial committee of the privy council which we know as the aviation and radio cases the constitutional atmosphere has been a good deal clarified in regard to the jurisdiction of this parliament and of the provincial legislatures in Canada. I had occasion once before, during the present session of this house, to discuss for a few moments some of the constitutional difficulties which have heretofore confronted us in the Dominion of Canada in regard to our constitutional act, and there is no doubt that until the decisions in the two cases I have just named there was considerable conflict of judicial opinion, in regard to many difficult and intricate questions under sections 91 and 92 of the British North America Act.
My hon. friend from Quebec (East (Mr. Lapointe) laboured for some time in an effort to distinguish those two cases, the aviation and radio cases, from the question dealt with in the resolution before the house. He has most fervently advanced the theory that in the aviation and radio cases Canada was bound by positive treaties and conventions. That is true, and the resolution before parliament to-day is the first step in bringing about another binding international convention, just as binding as the radio convention or the aviation treaty, which came about through the treaty of Versailles. My hon. friend from Quebec East must remember that the government now proposes, by this resolution, to adopt and eventually ratify the draft labour convention drawn up in Washington in 1919.
Reference has been made to opinions which I have hitherto expressed in regard to provincial jurisdiction in respect of hours of labour and, I think also in regard to minimum wages. Under the circumstances which existed at the time, I was correct in the views I expressed and I would not alter the opinions which I expressed on those occasions. I stick to them yet; they were right. There was no treaty or convention under consideration; there was no proposal to ratify a treaty or convention at that time. The resolution now before the house proposes the approval of a

convention which makes an entirely different problem. In 1924 when I expressed myself in regard to hours of labour nothing had been done towards the adoption of the draft convention which came to us from Washington in 1919. It was an academic ques'tion we were discussing; the opinion I then presented to the house was a correct opinion, and I stand by it to-day. When I spoke in 1932-and by the way, let me interject at this point that when I spoke on February 9 to the motion moved by Mr. Heenan in regard to minimum wages-

speechtext: No, the eight hour day

speechtext: Well, the same point was involved. When I spoke at that time I spoke without knowledge of the decisions of the judicial committee of the privy council in the two cases referred to. I think the hon. member for Quebec East at that time had no knowledge of them either.

maintopic: EIGHT HOUR DAY AND FORTY-EIGHT HOUR WEEK IN INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext: Yes, I had.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: EIGHT HOUR DAY AND FORTY-EIGHT HOUR WEEK IN INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext: We get newspaper and telegraphic reports that an appeal has been allowed or an appeal has been dismissed, together with a brief summary, but the report of the case does not reach Canada until months afterwards. maintopic: EIGHT HOUR DAY AND FORTY-EIGHT HOUR WEEK IN INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext: Is it not true that the Department of Justice receives copies of judgments long before the reports are issued?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: EIGHT HOUR DAY AND FORTY-EIGHT HOUR WEEK IN INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext: Not much before. We do receive them as a rule within six to eight weeks.

maintopic: EIGHT HOUR DAY AND FORTY-EIGHT HOUR WEEK IN INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext: I was there too. I know.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: EIGHT HOUR DAY AND FORTY-EIGHT HOUR WEEK IN INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext:
The radio case was, I think, decided just five or six days after I had spoken in the house. However, that is beside the point. I am now basing my opinion upon the fact that we propose to ratify this draft convention. The object of the resolution is to enable us to do so, and if the convention be ratified, as I assume it will be, then I submit that under our treaty making power in our constitutional act we have undoubtedly authority to pass the necessary legislation. If we do not intend to ratify the convention, and if it is merely to remain a dead letter as it has remained since 1919, then the opinions I expressed in the house in 1924 and 1934 I still hold. I believe they were correct. I place the question squarely before the house under section 132 of the British North America Act, and I have no hesitation in asserting jurisdiction for this parliament under that section.

International Labour Conventions
But it is not only upon that ground that jurisdiction may be claimed for the parliament of Canada in regard to this resolution. There is the matter of the regulation of trade and commerce within the dominion, and the matter of foreign trade. There is the establishment of equilibrium in matters of trade between the various provinces of the dominion. There can be little doubt that in all interprovincial trade and in all foreign trade this parliament has exclusive jurisdiction. I say on that among other grounds this legislation is justified, but in the meantime I am placing the matter before the house, so far as my opinion may carry weight, solely upon the ground of our constitutional right to bind the provinces and bind Canada under the authority of section 132 of the British North America Act.

maintopic: EIGHT HOUR DAY AND FORTY-EIGHT HOUR WEEK IN INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this afternoon we have listened to the observations of three of the most eminent legal gentlemen in the Dominion of Canada. As an ordinary layman I can speak with very little knowledge or authority on constitutional questions; my understanding of them is limited. I did however upon one occasion have some practice in criminal law. In the year 1919, to which reference has been made so often to-day, along with six other persons I stood at the bar of justice, and while there I got a little insight into criminal proceedings. For reasons I do not desire now to explain I defended my own case, acting as my own lawyer. Most of the accused had the benefit of legal counsel. All those who had legal counsel were found guilty. Some few weeks after the trial I met the late Judge Metcalfe, whom some hon. members would know, and discussing the case he said, "Heaps, it is a good thing for you that you had no lawyer defending you; if you had you would have gone to gaol along with the rest." So when it comes to questions of lawyers and legal opinions I am sometimes sceptical of the luminaries and the stacks of books and precedents brought forward in an effort to seek something from the musty past and to adjust it to modem conditions.
I was deeply interested in the splendid presentation of the case by the former Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe). I sincerely hope and trust that when he speaks about a forty hour week, or a week even shorter than that, he speaks for his party particularly in the province of Quebec. Next week when the government introduces the bill providing for a forty-eight hour week I am sure he, along with other hon. members, will have an opportunity to vote for a shorter working week than at present obtains, and that it be
provided for in the bill. I sincerely hope we shall be able to cooperate in asking for a thirty hour week, or as a compromise a thirty-four hour week. I hope such a proposal will have his support and the support of many [DOT]other hon. members.

maintopic: EIGHT HOUR DAY AND FORTY-EIGHT HOUR WEEK IN INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext: Why work at all?

maintopic: EIGHT HOUR DAY AND FORTY-EIGHT HOUR WEEK IN INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext:
To-day we have heard about the radio and aviation cases, but I believe there is a case which is more important than those, namely, the case of the millions of Canadian people who are to-day looking for remedial measures and a way out of the difficulties in which they find themselves. Of course we realize the importance of our constitution and the British North America Act. At this point may I say, along with the former Minister of Justice, that I am as much prepared as he is to respect the rights of minorities, and particularly those in his own province. I will go as far as he goes in defending the rights of the people in his province. I believe a discussion of the needs of the people of Canada is of greater importance than a discussion of the British North America Act.
It has been pointed out this afternoon that the opinions of legal luminaries change with changing conditions, and I believe it was pointed out further that a recent judicial decision had changed one which had been given formerly, and made legal that which was formerly illegal. For two reasons I am pleased that the government has seen fit to bring in this legislation. First of all, assuming the legislation is legal, it will give centralized authority in the dominion, so far as hours of labour are concerned. There can be no doubt that centralized authority is essential, if we are to have anything approaching harmonious understanding between the Canadian provinces. For instance, we cannot have men and women in one part of the dominion working fifty or sixty hours a week and in another part, in similar industries, working only forty-four hours. Only this morning I received a communication which I have forwarded to the proper minister. It contained the information that a dominion contract has been called for. A western manufacturer complains that in certain eastern factories employees are working for wages as lowr as twenty cents an hour, whereas in the western provinces the wages are twenty-five to thirty per cent higher. Naturally we cannot have such a condition of affairs continue in the Dominion of Canada.
Then I am glad for another reason, Mr. Speaker, that legislation of this character is introduced. It shows that this parliament is beginning to recognize that the limitation of

International Labour Conventions
working hours is essential so far as Canada is concerned. This is the first time, I believe, that parliament has gone on record through legislation dealing with a maximum working week; it is the first recognition by parliament that such a limitation of working hours is in the best interests of the Dominion of Canada.
My good friend the former Minister of Justice spoke of labour and a new deal, and then he brought in the constitution. In other words, Mr. Speaker, the implication is that the British North America Act is of greater consequence, of more importance to the people of this dominion than a new deal. I am not for one moment arguing whether what the government is proposing is a good thing or a bad thing. Personally I am inclined very much to the opinion of the former Minister of Justice. I do not think that a forty-eight hour week begins to touch the situation, so far as the hours of labour are concerned in this dominion. Nevertheless it is a recognition of certain principles, and because of that we are compelled to support the resolution and the bill which will be brought before the house. But when my hon. friend the former Minister of Justice speaks of a new deal, and then at once throws in its way all the constitutional difficulties he can possibly think of, I would ask how are we ever going to get a new deal if we are always to put the constitution ahead of it? In other words, we can never have a new deal unless, as I have said before, we recognize that the British North America Act was made for the people of Canada and not the people of Canada for the British North America Act.

speechtext: I am sure my hon. friend does not wish to misinterpret me.

maintopic: EIGHT HOUR DAY AND FORTY-EIGHT HOUR WEEK IN INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext: I certainly do not.

speechtext: If he will allow me, what I said, and what I still say, is that this should be done but that it should be done in a proper and constitutional way. I am not throwing the constitution in the way. I said that we should make the necessary amendments or come to the necessary understanding. The thing will be better if it is well done.

maintopic: EIGHT HOUR DAY AND FORTY-EIGHT HOUR WEEK IN INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext:
Yes. It is only a question of interpretation of the powers of parliament, and I suggest that perhaps the lawyers who have considered this legislation have given it just as much consideration as my hon. friend who has just taken his seat. Legal gentlemen may not agree upon a certain interpretation, but the members of the government feel that what they are doing is the right and proper way to proceed, and I am glad they are taking

hold of the situation in the way they are; let those who oppose this form of legislation come out in the open and say they oppose it.
We talk about the rights of parliament and the sovereignty of the constitution, but when we speak of sovereignty one thing that should not be forgotten is the sovereignty of the people. The sovereignty of the people should be supreme. So in matters of this kind, while I respect the constitution and want to see things done in a constitutional way, I say we cannot ignore the demands of the people of the Dominion of Canada; for if we allow our constitution to be so rigid and inflexible, it will break down and cause no end of chaos in this dominion. To-day we find that there are representations from all sections of the country and from every shade of opinion in the country to the effect that the rights which the government are taking upon themselves at the present time should be exercised by this parliament, and that such questions as hours of labour and a minimum wage should be and probably are a matter of federal right instead of provincial.
My hon. friend from Quebec East read from certain laws that have recently been passed in the province of Quebec relating to the building industry and a forty hour week. I am glad that the province of Quebec has recognized a forty hour week, and in a sense I approve of that legislation. The reason no doubt they made it a forty hour instead of a forty-eight hour week in the building industry in the province of Quebec was that the men were not even working a ten hour week on the average, and so nobody was hurt by that legislation. But I venture to assert that the province of Quebec did not bring in any legislation providing for a forty hour week in those industries in which at the very moment we are sitting here employees are working fifty-five and sixty hours a week-such industries and trades, for instance, as have been investigated during the past few months. What conditions were found in those industries? Girls were working fifty-five and sixty hours a week; and in the whole of the province of Quebec I think the information came out that they had only one or two inspectors to enforce some of these laws. It is one thing to have laws on the statute books, but it is another thing when it comes to enforcing them. If laws of this kind are to be made effective it can be done only when you have not the competition that exists to-day as between province and province only when the whole matter is dealt with uniformly right across the dominion. If we have power to put this legislation into effect I hope that the laws that we pass will be strictly enforced

International Labour Conventions
by the proper authorities. But if we are going to allow the judiciary, as has been suggested, to interpret at all times what the laws really are and what the constitution of the country is, who is going to be sovereign in this Dominion of Canada? Is it to be parliament and the people, or is it to be the judiciary as it is in the United States? I for one would hate to see this country put in the same position as the United States where if a certain law is not liked by a group of individuals it has to go before the supreme court of the United States for-shall I say?-its endorsation; and in reality it is the supreme court of the United States which in the final analysis dictates what the laws are that are passed by congress. Personally I want to see this parliament supreme and representing the people. I do not like the judiciary interpreting the law too much. In fact, I do not like them at all when it comes to a question of interpreting the law. I would rather see that left to parliament to deal with, as it is in Great Britain. You do not see a great many judicial interpretations of the law in Great Britain.
I had not intended to speak on this question at all, Mr. Speaker, and I was prompted to do so only by what was said by the former Minister of Justice. However, I am extremely glad that this legislation is being brought down, because as I said when the resolution on unemployment insurance was before the house last week, I attach far more importance to the shorter working day and increased wages than to the bill dealing with unemployment insurance. I do not regard the forty-eight hour iveek as a panacea for any of the problems which are facing us at the present time, but if the forty-eight hour week is reduced to about a thirty hour week we shall be going a long way towards solving some of the difficulties through which this country is passing at the present time. I am glad to give this legislation my endorsation. A great many things have happened since 1919, and to-day when the house is being asked to approve of a forty-eight hour week I may say that the forty-eight hour week or the eight hour day is as obsolete in 1935 as the twelve hour day was in 1919. I hope that when the measure is brought down dealing with the forty-eight hour week, amendments will be permitted looking towards a shorter working day and a shorter working week, and that such amendments will receive the sympathetic consideration of this House of Commons.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in
view of the length of the discussion and the wide range it has necessarily taken, it may be well to remind the house that what we have 92582-42
before us at the moment is not a bill providing for an eight hour day, of which the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) has given notice, but a draft convention of the general conference of the international labour organization. It is that draft convention which this house is being asked to approve. I will read the resolution so that it will be clear in the minds of all present:
That, it is expedient that parliament do approve of the convention limiting the hours of work in industrial undertakings to eight in the day and forty-eight in the week adopted as a draft convention by the general conference of the international labour organization of the League of Nations at its first session in Washington on the 28th day of November, 1919, reading as follows:
This afternoon we approved of four draft conventions of the international labour organization. We have approved of all of them in the light of what we believe to be the legislative competence of this parliament, and we have approved of them to the extent of that competence. We on this side are prepared to approve of the draft convention now before us with respect to hours of labour in exactly the same way and on exactly the same terms. We approve of the draft convention so far as the legislative competence of this parliament permits us to do so, in other words in so far as the jurisdiction of this parliament is concerned.
There is one thing above all else which is important in this as in all matters of public relations and human affairs, and that is for us to be at least honest with ourselves as members of parliament, honest with those whom we represent, and particularly as members desirous of promoting social reform to be honest with those whose interest we hope to be able to further by any action we may take in this parliament. There come to my mind in this connection the words of the exMinister of Justice, my hon. friend from Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe), when he said that an assumption of jurisdiction does not create jurisdiction. I think it is important that we should all remember that. I might change the word "assumption" to the word "assertion" and say that an assertion of jurisdiction does not confer jurisdiction. Nor does the assertion of legislative competence confer legislative competence, even if that assertion is made by the present Minister of Justice or by the Prime Minister; that does not make the least bit of difference. Legislative competence is either here or it is not here, and when the matter comes to be decided it will be decided by that branch of government which exists for the purpose of settling questions of legislative competence. The Prime



International Labour Conventions
Minister has repeatedly and most emphatically said that of the different branches of government he regards the judicial as the most important, and he has given as his reason for that opinion the fact that the judicial branch is the one that determines these very questions of legislative competence. So that whatever we do here is done in the light of what we believe to be our legislative competence. If I believed that the courts of the land when the competence of any of this legislation came to be decided were going to present a certain point of view, I should feel it my duty to bring that fact to the attention of those who are interested in the legislation. And as leader of the opposition in parliament it is part of my duty with respect to the legislation which has been introduced to point out any feature which is likely at present to be misunderstood or to which exception later is likely to be taken. I should be very much remiss in my duty as leader of the opposition if I did not reemphasize what has been so ably said this afternoon by my colleague, the ex-Minister of Justice, with reference to jurisdiction, if I did not reemphasize what has already been given as the opinion of all ministers of justice who have held office in this country since the League of Nations was created, as well as the opinion which have been given by the Supreme Court of Canada. I need not say more than that.
I should perhaps point out to my hon. friend from North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps), who has just spoken, that I entirely agree with him when he urges the desirability of uniformity in legislation as between the provinces and as between the dominion and the provinces. Unquestionably uniformity of labour standards is something to be desired, and it is to be desired not in the field of Canada alone, because the whole purpose of these conventions is to bring about uniformity so far as may be possible throughout the world. It is not going to help Canada, as much as we should like to see her helped, for her to have the best standards, though they may be uniform, if other countries have lower standards. Unfortunately, as my hon. friend knows better than anyone else perhaps, where there are two standards competing with each other the baser of the two is apt to prevail in the long run. It has therefore been the hope of those interested in labour matters at Geneva that they would be able to bring about such uniformity of laws that those countries with high standards would not suffer by reason of their virtue and that the mean country would not profit in virtue of its meanness. That
fMr. Mackenzie King.]
is the whole purpose underlying uniformity. But there are two ways of bringing uniformity about.
I think the tragedy of this parliament has been that though we have been here through five sessions at a time when labour matters were to the fore and when the provinces as well as the dominion were all in a mood to work together for improving industrial conditions, there has been no conference between the provinces and the dominion that amounted to anything with respect to labour legislation. Two or three conferences have been called but they have been over night affairs; representatives of the provincial governments have come here from the different provinces to discuss certain measures and on their arrival they have been asked by the ministry what their views were with regard to certain questions, without the ministry telling them anything about its views. With respect to this very question of the hours of labour there was a conference no more recently than two years ago, and when the representatives from all the different provinces came the question wras:	which of your
rights are you prepared to give up? We wish to know that before we proceed any further. That was the substance of the remarks addressed to them by the Prime Minister himself.

speechtext:
Yes, but I am referring to the conference prior to that; the same thing occurred at the conference. They were asked what they were prepared to surrender. Some were quite prepared to surrender certain of their rights but they wanted a quid pro quo; they wished to know in the taking over of services who was going to foot the bill. Others were not prepared to surrender anything and no decision was reached. Had a real effort been made during these five years to bring into conference the different provinces of the dominion with a view to securing uniformity with respect to the shortening of the working day, there would not have been any trouble in attaining that end, and we should now have had an eight hour day and a forty-eight hour week effective in the various trades from one end of Canada to the other.
May I point out further that, as the exMinister of Justice said, there are different ways of going about things. We are living under a parliamentary system of government. Whatever we may be in the course of the

International Labour Conventions
next year, we are at present not a full-fledged dictatorship. The method by which we have hoped-some of us at least-to effect reforms in this country for some time to come is the parliamentary method. It would be an unhappy day for labour in this country if it ever began to hope for its reforms from a dictatorship. They might seemingly gain something until they themselves became members of the servile state. Once members of the servile state they would soon find out where they stood under a system of regimentation, with a dictator at the head of affairs. So long as we have a parliamentary system of government, a constitution which governs the country, there should be observance of the proper methods of procedure with respect to effecting any changes that may be necessary. Therein lies the second great tragedy, it seems to me, of this parliament's failure to proceed as it might have done in these matters. If there had been a conference, as it was repeatedly suggested from this side there should be, to consider this very question of jurisdiction, this very question of amendments to the British North America Act, what would appear to be necessary in the way of amendments to the act might have been known at least four years ago and steps could long ago have been taken to have the act amended wherein it may be necessary to amend it. Had that been done, we would not have had to-day to wait for what amendments may be necessary to the British North America Act to effect certain purposes much to be desired, for agreement between the provinces and the dominion to effect a desired result; all that would have been settled long before this.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) has been one of those who along with hon. members of the opposition have urged upon the government during each of the past five sessions that the provinces be called into conference with a view to taking steps at once to have the British North America Act so amended as to give us power in these social matters to legislate as may be necessary. But his appeals and those from this side have fallen on deaf ears. Unfortunate as this may be, we have to look the facts in the face. The mere making of assertions as to what is or is not to be does not meet the situation in any way that can be at all helpful. It may help to serve the purposes of a general election, although I do not believe it will even do that. But a very serious situation for labour and the country will arise if the legislation which we are passing in this parliament dealing
with great social problems should all of a sudden come to naught because of the fact that instead of building our house upon a rock we are building it upon sand, and instead of building upon truth we are building upon error. Some of us want to avoid that kind of situation. We wish to see these reforms put through, but on a solid, enduring and truthful basis; and it is on that ground alone that we are prepared to support them.
As to the eight hour day and the approval of this house, I imagine there are some hon. members who have forgotten and probably some who never knew that as long ago as 1910 this house approved the principle of the eight hour day. We had in the parliament of 1908 to 1911 Mr. Alphonse Verville, of the city of Montreal, who like my hon. friend was a representative of labour. Mr. Verville brought in on one or two occasions a bill for an eight hour day with respect to public works and undertakings of the federal government. His bill for one reason or another did not get support the first year or two, but may I say that when I had the honour of being taken into Sir Wilfrid Laurier's cabinet as Minister of Labour and Mr. Verville reintroduced his bill, I moved in the house that the bill should be referred to a special committee to deal with the question of hours of labour on public works. I was subsequently elected chairman of that committee, and I have in my hand a copy of the report of its proceedings: proceedings of the special committee on Bill No. 21, an act respecting hours of labour on public works, comprising reports, evidence and correspondence, December 9, 1909, to May 3, 1910. This, as one may see, is a voluminous compendium, comprising between 700 and 800 pages, but as I recall the matter, and as the proceedings record, we had not concluded the taking of evidence at the end of that session. Next session, when Mr. Verville reintroduced his bill, instead of having the committee go over the matter further, the House of Commons passed the bill through its different stages. I supported it very strongly, maintaining the principle of an eight hour day for labour on all federal government undertakings or on whatever might come within the legislative competence of this parliament. As I have said, the bill passed the House of Commons. Therefore this house approved the eight hour day principle at that time. The bill went to the Senate; it passed its first reading and its second reading there, so that the Senate approved the principle of the eight hour day. After second reading in the Senate the bill

International Labour Conventions
was referred to a committee. As happened in respect to another measure of which I spoke this afternoon, dissolution took place suddenly on the reciprocity issue before a report had been made by the Senate committee, and the legislation was not enacted at that time. But as a result of the discussion and of the action taken then, the government from that time on-I am speaking now of Liberal administrations, although I think the same is true of the administration that followed that of Sir Wilfrid Laurier-construed the fair wages resolution which had been passed by this house, and which related to wages and hours on government work, as one which should fix as a maximum number of hours for work, the eight hour day. I speak subject to correction, but my impression is that the Labour department gave that construction to what was meant by a fair day's work-an eight hour day-and the schedules that were attached to the various contracts fixed the day at eight hours.

speechtext:
The Prime
Minister says: "Not until later." He may be right, because as all hon. members know, after 1911 we passed to the decade which was the period of the war, and certainly during the war it may well be that in some cases longer hours were permitted. But after the war I think the eight hour day principle was pretty generally observed. At any rate I can speak for the administration of which I was the head from 1921 to 1930. Throughout that time the Labour department felt itself bound by the fair wages resolution as we interpreted it and by orders in council as we passed them, to give effect to the eight hour day with respect to government work. As has been referred to this afternoon by the exMinister of Justice, our government did not stop at public works and undertakings-and it will be noticed that this draft convention relates to industrial undertakings-the government took in the public service generally in its endeavour to further the principle of the eight hour day. I think I should read the order in council that was passed. It was referred to by the ex-Minister of Justice, but I think it should be placed on record in full because it shows to what extent the late Liberal administration at any rate was prepared to support the eight hour day principle generally. It is P.C. 670, approved by the governor general on March 27, 1930, and was laid on the table of the house on March 31, 1930, as reported on pages 10S2 and 1083 of Hansard:
[Mr. Mackenzie King.l
The committee of the privy council have had before them a report, dated 19th March, 1930, from the Minister of Labour, submitting as follows.
May I say that this and one other order in council summed up what there had been in the form of regulations during the previous years and put them in the form of formal orders in council.
1.	That it was recognized in the labour part of the treaty of Versailles and the corresponding provisions of the other treaties of peace, that the wellbeing-physical, moral and intellectual- of industrial wage earners is of supreme international importance, and that although differences of climate, habits and customs, economic principles and industrial traditions, make strict uniformity in the conditions of labour difficult of immediate attainment, there are methods and principles for regulating labour conditions which all industrial communities should endeavour to apply, so far as their special circumstances will permit.
2.	That approval was expressed in the peace treaties of the principle of the eight hour working day.
3.	That a draft convention was adopted at the first session of the conference of the international labour organization (League of Nations) in 1919 to limit hours of work in industrial undertakings to eight hours per day.
4.	That the draft convention above mentioned was referred in 1924 to the select standing committee on industrial and international relations of the House of Commons of Canada for examination and report.
5.	That on the recommendation of the committee on industrial and international relations of the House of Commons, approved by the House of Commons, the draft convention on hours of work in industrial undertakings was referred by order in council to the Supreme Court of Canada with a view to determining the jurisdiction of the federal and provincial authorities, respectively, on this subject.
May I point out that this is the very draft convention which is -before us at the present time. It was referred to a select committee of the house, and the committee, of which I think my hon. friend was a member, on which at any rate all parties in this house were represented, were unanimous in their decision that the matter should be referred to the supreme court for an opinion. And the members were unanimous as well in their approval of the principle of the eight hour day. So again this house approved in that manner the principle of the eight hour day. The order in council continues:
G. That the judgment of the Supreme Court of Canada contained the following declaration: "The subject matter is generally within the competence of the -legislatures of the provinces but the authority vested in these legislatures does not enable them to give the force of law to provisions such as those contained in the draft convention in relation to servants of the dominion government, or to legislate for those parts of Canada which are not within the boundaries of a province."

International Labour Conventions
7.	That a report from the Civil Service Commission, which was submitted to Your Excellency in Council under date of February 16, 1925. showed that the standard daily hours of work of monthly rate employees in the government department are from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., with an interval for luncheon and a halfholiday on Saturday, and that the standard hours of prevailing rate employees, numbering 1,576 in Ottawa and 18,264 outside Ottawa (of whom 12.247 were postmasters paid on percentage basis), are 44 hours per week, based on an eight hour day for five days, and 4 hours, or a half day, on Saturday. Certain exceptions to these standard hours of work were also noted in the report of the Civil Service Commission.
8.	That request has been made to the government for the granting of the eight hour day to its own employees.
9.	That it is desirable that the principle of the eight hour day should be applied to any branches of the public service of Canada in which it is not now observed.
The minister accordingly recommends that, except in cases where the work of employees is intermittent in character, or the application of this rule is not deemed to be practicable or in the public interest, the hours of work of any employees of the dominion government who are still required to work more than eight hours daily be reduced to eight hours daily, with a half holiday on Saturday.
The committee concur in the foregoing recommendation and submit the same for approval.
E. J. Lemaire,
Clerk of the Privy Council.
That order in council was approved, and as I have pointed out it extends the principle to the public service as set forth in its provisions.
But the late Liberal administration did not stop there. One of the last measures that was enacted before we went out of office was the passing of an eight hour day act. I have in my hand the text of the measure;
An act respecting fair wages and an eight hour day for labour employed on public works of the Dominion of Canada.
1.	This act may be cited as The Fair Wages and Eight Hour Day Act, 1930.
2.	In this act the expression "minister" means the Minister of Labour.
3.	(1) Every contract made hereafter with the government of Canada for construction, remodelling, repair or demolition of any work shall be subject to the following conditions respecting wages and hours:
(a)	All persons in the employ of the contractor, sub-contractor, or of any other person doing or contracting to do the whole or any part of the work contemplated by the contract shall be paid such wages as are generally accepted as current from time to time for competent workmen in the district in which the work is being performed for the character or class of work in which they are respectively engaged; provided that wages shall in all oases be 6uch as are fair and reasonable;
(b)	the working hours of persons while so employed 6hall not exceed eight hours per day except in such special cases as the governor in council may otherwise provide, or except in cases of emergency, as may be approved by the minister.
Then there are other particulars which help to make more definite that provision, and there is one which says;
The governor in council, on the recommendation of the minister, may make regulations with regard to wages and hours herein provided for and without limiting the generality of the foregoing may provide by regulation for-
And a series of provisions or sections are set out all of which are intended to ensure the carrying out of the letter as well as the spirit of that legislation.
So I may sum up by saying that as long ago as 1910, this House of Commons approved the principle of an eight hour day to the extent of its legislative competence and authority; that again 'by its interpretation of the resolution respecting the payment of fair wages and the application of hours and fair conditions in connection with public works it has approved it, and that by order in council and by legislation, as I have already stated, it has approved it. So far, therefore, as this resolution is concerned as it comes to this parliament from Geneva via the government, in the light of orders in council read this afternoon, which still stand, because they have not been repealed, I think this house should have no difficulty whatever in approving the draft convention. Certainly those of us who belong to the Liberal party are only too ready to approve it in those terms.

speechtext:
Listening to this discussion reminded me of the story told about Galileo, who, tortured on the rack for saying that the world moves, recanted, but in an aside said that it moves for all that. I am inclined to agree with Galileo, that the world does move. The right hon. gentleman who has just taken hit seat (Mr. Mackenzie King) stated that his government began the agitation for the eight hour day in 1910. In 1919 the international labour organization took it up, and now almost sixteen years later it has come up here for approval. Surely we are making progress 1 As the right hon. gentleman said, I cannot see at the moment what particular useful purpose our approval can serve, unless it be for election purposes. But I noticed, when he was telling us of the achievements of the Liberal government, that the order in council he read was passed on March 27, 1930, just a short time before the dissolution of parliament. So I presume that the present government has learned something from the government that preceded them.
The eight hour day is obsolete to-day. I have before me the legislative program of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada placed
662	COMMONS
International Labour Conventions
before the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) and members of the cabinet in 1932. In the paragraph referring to hours of labour I find this:
For the past ten years requests have been submitted seeking compliance by Canada with the eight hour day convention of the international labour office.
Then it goes on to point out that this has been submitted to the Supreme Court of Canada for decision. Now for ten years, that is ever since 1922 when the Liberal party came into office, the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada have been trying to have this convention approved. There is no reason why we should oppose this resolution, but unless we do something more than just approve we are not doing anything. For the last four or five years the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada at their conventions have gone on record in favour not of the eight hour day and the forty-eight hour week but of the six hour day and five day week, which as a matter of fact has been adopted already in some instances. If we are going to put the unemployed workers of this country back at work; if the unemployed workers in all the industrial countries of the world are to be employed again, we will have to go further, possibly, than the six hour day and five day week.
Looking in this direction the right hon. leader of the opposition stated that labour had nothing to gain from a dictatorship. I should like to point out to the right hon. gentleman that if and when a dictatorship comes in this country it is far more likely to come through the owning classes than through the labour movement. If there is any movement in this dominion that is opposed to a dictatorship I would say it is the labour movement. That is not only true of Canada; it is true of other countries as well. The people who have financed the dictatorship in other capitalist countries have been the owning and the ruling classes of those countries, so the right hon. gentleman need not concern himself with whether or not we are in favour of dictatorship.
