speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: EIGHT HOUR DAY AND FORTY-EIGHT HOUR WEEK IN INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not know just why
so much heat and feeling should be introduced into this debate. To me it is the discussion of a matter of very great interest, which should not arouse any animosities and which should not be the occasion for the expression of so much bitterness.
In the first place objection was taken with regard to the form of the resolution. I said that I would look it up this evening at recess, and I find that my recollection was correct. When the resolution was being prepared I suggested that it should be in the terms of the resolution introduced by the right hon. gentleman (Mr. Mackenzie King) when dealing with exactly the same situation in 1928. In the journals of that year I find the following:
On motion of Mr. Mackenzie King (Prince Albert) it was resolved,-That it is expedient that parliament do approve of the slavery convention signed at Geneva on the twenty-fifth of September, one thousand nine hundred and twenty-six, and which was signed, on behalf of Canada, by the Canadian representative duly authorized to that effect;
And that this house do approve of same.
That applied also with respect to two other resolutions, one with respect to an international sanitary convention and the other dealing with another matter. I mention these because I thought it desirable that we should have a uniform form of resolution-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: EIGHT HOUR DAY AND FORTY-EIGHT HOUR WEEK IN INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext: I agree.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: EIGHT HOUR DAY AND FORTY-EIGHT HOUR WEEK IN INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext:
-and I am responsible to that extent for the resolution being in its present form. I still think it was better to follow the form used by the right hon. gentleman than the form which was suggested this afternoon. On further consideration I think it is correct to say that it is expedient that parliament should pass it and that this house should take the necessary action in that direction.
So much for that point. May I again suggest to the right hon. gentleman that he is hardly fair to himself when he suggests that during the last few years an interprovincial conference might have been held at which these matters might have been disposed of. The right hon. gentleman was in power in prosperous times, when the difficulties of the great depression were not overhanging all government activities. Yet from 1921 to 1930 I find it difficult to discover anywhere in the record anything that would indicate that

International Labour Conventions
unity or unanimity was secured as between the provinces and the dominion with respect to any matters of this character. I am not unmindful of the fact that an interprovincial conference was held; I am not unmindful of the fact that it laboured for many days; I am not unmindful of the fact that the results were negligible.
I also have to remind this house that I have never thought it necessary that a long time should be taken in disposing of conferences. We called the conference to deal with the statute of Westminster, and let me remind this house that had that statute been passed in the terms suggested by the former Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) it would have done violence to the rights of a part of this dominion. In consequence of the objection of the provinces, commencing with Ontario, at the conference of 1930 I asked that section 7, dealing with the Canadian situation, should be allowed to stand until I could send over a draft of the section. On my return to Canada a draft section was prepared in our office, with the assistance of others as well as of myself, and we called a conference. That conference met at ten o'clock in the morning. The next day the initials of every premier of Canada had been appended to the section in approval; in one case it was the representative of the premier, but that included the premiers of Quebec and Ontario. That was done in less than thirty-six hours. If you have prepared something; if you know what you want to do and have an opportunity for a frank and full discussion, there is no reason why it should not be done as it was on that occasion. At every conference we have held since 1930 we have had definite proposals to submit to the provinces when they attended. They have expressed their views and we have been prompt in signifying our approval or disapproval of their suggestions, and the conferences have terminated. Always they have sat just as long as it was desirable to sit in order to do the business. No purpose is ever served by having conferences last longer than is necessary to dispose of the business with which they have to deal.
May I further remind this house that the matter to which the right hon. gentleman referred, namely insurance, was a matter about which there had been grave differences of opinion. Following the Citizens Insurance Company and Parsons case back in the early days the privy council had determined by a long series of decisions that the business of insurance was under the exclusive legislative jurisdiction of the provinces. Yet three of
the provinces at the conferences we held expressed not only their willingness but their desire that we should take over insurance from them, because they, felt they had neither the machinery nor the revenues with which adequately to deal with the matter, having regard to the magnitude of the business itself. But the older provinces were not so inclined, with the result that the discussion did not bring about any fruitful result. Nor will such discussions bring about any fruitful result so long as the greater provinces, and particularly the largest of all, believe they have quite as much ability as we have and have the legislative competence to deal with insurance, and continue to do so.
I mention that in passing because there was also another matter under discussion, namely companies. We did agree, and I am happy to say that it was unanimous so far as the provinces and the dominion were concerned, that we should have a uniform Companies Act. But when it came down to terms there was such a difference of opinion that it was impossible to arrive at any uniform act which was acceptable to all.
With respect to other problems with which we had to deal we were able to arrive at conclusions very speedily. I do in all fairness submit to this house that if during these long years of toil and depression, where we have been able to bring about a measure of agreement with the provinces in connection with so vital a matter as the statute of Westminster and with respect to other matters with which we have had to deal, arising out of the depression, we are hardly censurable compared with those who had ten years or thereabouts to deal with these problems and -bring about a solution of them by unanimous agreement with the provinces.
I might also say that when the case to which we have been referring this aftemon with respect to hours of labour was argued before the Supreme Court of Canada the position taken by the province of Ontario was a very simple one. They said this:
Edward Bayly, K.C., appearing for the Attorney General of Ontario, argued that the dominion parliament has exclusive power to sanction ratification of the draft convention of the international labour conference, and that if a draft convention is formally ratified, thereupon becoming binding upon the dominion, a further obligation will rest upon the dominion authorities to take whatever action is necessary to make its provisions effective. In the absence of ratification of the eight hour day convention by the federal authorities, it was contended' on behalf of the province of Ontario that its subject matter is probably within provincial legis lative control.

International Labour Conventions
So that if we are to apportion blame on the basis of non-intervention by way of effective effort it will clearly appear that within the argument made by the province of Ontario before the Supreme Court of Canada the lack of attention was on the part of the federal government for not ratifying the convention and thereby making it a federal law. That in itself explains not only why it has not heretofore been regarded as a federal matter, but also why we are now seeking ratification before following it with a legislative enactment, notice of which appears on the order paper.
I do not propose to do more than make one observation with respect to one statement of the former Minister of Justice. I refer to the letter which I sent to the provinces last year. Of course he realized when he was reading it I was putting before the provinces the position which they had taken. We have had frequent discussions about this at various conferences, informally. I was surprised to hear the right hon. gentleman suggest that in any sense we were endeavouring to compel them to do anything. There were informal discussions with respect to the legislative capacity of the legislatures in connection with social matters as distinguished from the power of the parliament of Canada. Frequently that was the discussion in general terms. The letter which I sent out in August or the early part of September, 1934, to all the premiers was predicated upon putting before them the position which I understood they took and which I believe is really the position which many of them did take, although I do not think the province of Ontario did take it as strongly as has been suggested, namely that they claimed exclusive jurisdiction. It has always been a subject matter of discussion as to the terms on which they were willing to part with it-and I refer to old age pensions and matters of that kind. I was not endeavouring to express an opinion in that letter, because my opinions have never been expressed to them in those terms.
But there was another matter which arose. A conference was to be called. During my absence an effort to raise issues was made by the premier of Quebec, and again in an editorial in the Vancouver Sun; and at the meeting at whioh the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Howden) accepted his nomination he said that we were going to endeavour to raise racial and religious issues at that conference. When I came back and asked the various premiers-I do not wonder the hon. gentleman smiles-whether they were prepared to meet in conference, one of them said he could not come before Christmas, and I

advised by telegram every one of them, and made a statement in the press that such action had been taken. I would deprecate any effort to raise the issues mentioned in the editorial in the Vancouver Sun, or the warning given at his nomination convention by the hon. member for St. Boniface. I.mention this in passing-

speechtext: I do not remember any such warning.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: EIGHT HOUR DAY AND FORTY-EIGHT HOUR WEEK IN INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext:
All he has to do is to read his speech when he accepted nomination, and if he will do that 'I will make it right for him in this house if he does not find that what I have said is correct.
To proceed further: There are three propositions I desire to make to this house. The first one is this, that on the issue as to the question which we now submit should be decided in the affirmative, as to the jurisdiction of this parliament, the Journal of Comparative Legislation and International Law of November, 1934 contains an article upon the constitutional capacity of Canada to give effect to an international labour conference. Mr. Jenks, in his article, refers to the observations of Mr. Justice, now Chief Justice Duff, in dealing with the question of jurisdiction. Mr. Justice Duff after dealing with article 405 made this reservation of some importance:
No question is submitted as to the duty of the member arising under the succeeding clauses of the same article in the event of the competent authority or authorities giving its or their consent to the recommendation or draft convention; and upon this no opinion is expressed.
Mr. Jenks proceeded in his discussion to point out that no question was asked of the Supreme Court of Canada as to the competence of this parliament. He said:
The direct question: "Is the dominion competent under any provision of the British North America Act to enact legislation giving effect to the convention?" was never properly before the court.
And it was not. Then arguments were lodged in favour of the dominion jurisdiction, and at one point, as an instance of the strange anomalies of life, the dominion joined with the province of Quebec and argued against its own jurisdiction. That is disclosed by the record.
I am not concerned about the arguments; I am not concerned about the theories; I am concerned only about one thing, namely the practical question. I think one can speak to it without any difficulty. I could not help but think in the Socratic method: as the

International Labour Conventions
hon. gentleman was arguing: Did the government sign on behalf of the British empire the treaty of peace? With the provisions with respect to labour that I urged this afternoon the answer to that must be yes. That is clear.
There is just one further point to which for some reason the hon. gentleman this afternoon would not refer. Article 405 in the treaty reads in part:
In the case of a federal state, the power of which to enter into conventions on labour matters is subject to limitations, it shall be in the discretion of that government to treat a draft convention to which such limitations apply as a recommendation only, and the provisions of this article with respect to recommendations shall apply in such case.
Therefore there was -conferred upon the government of the day a discretion. That discretion the Liberal government exercised by making recommendations to the provinces and ultimately making a reference to the courts in which, as Mr. Jenks said, the direct question was never settled. This government proposes to exercise the discretion in the opposite sense. We propose to exercise a discretion by exercising our legislative powers and passing legislation after ratification of the convention. That is all there is to it.
I do not think that the problem of law is as obstructive and as difficult as might be suggested. The only reason I read from the judgment this afternoon was a very simple one, namely so that members of the House of Commons who are interested in reading these matters, and many of them are, might at least have before them the decisions of the court in that regard. They would have before them the statements made by the judges in arriving at their conclusion and the reasons which governed their action.
Now, Canada claims to be a nation; Canada signs conventions; Canada makes treaties. The ex-Minister of Justice, who spoke this afternoon, signed the Halibut treaty as a minister, and as the Minister of Justice for Canada. We have claimed, and rightly claimed, that under the pow'ers conferred upon us we have become a nation. (Tf we are a nation there must be somewhere in this national government-and I do not use the term "national government" in the sense in which it is sometimes used-in this national federal government there must !be somewhere a power to speak for all the citizens of Canada. That being so, as Lord Sankey said, certainly no one province can do it. Certainly you cannot piece it together by saying that in the aggregate all the provinces can do it. But the body corporate,
the entity, is the Dominion of Canada, and that dominion speaks through this parliament with respect to matters to which we have bound ourselves by our treaty obligations.
I submit with deference that the former Minister of Justice has confused the words "obligation" and "power". The question of power is the question of jurisdiction. The question of obligation is the acceptance of responsibility. The dominion does not accept the responsibility except through the execution of a treaty. If it accepts that responsibility in the exercise of a discretion then the power is conferred by section 132. When the obligation is accepted the power is conferred by that section 132. It is so simple. It is like an ordinary everyday agreement. If a man is willing to accept an obligation it follows that he has the power to do it, or the obligation should not be made.
Now the treaty of Versailles provides for two things: (a) the renunciation by taking action of a national obligation-, or in the case of a discretion (b) the acceptance of the obligation If the nation accepts the obligation, then the power is found in section 132. Side by side with the responsibility marches the jurisdiction to exercise it. That jurisdiction may or may not be exercised, but there is the power to exercise it. During the last sixteen years this parliament was not asked to ratify the convention. It might have been; it was not. What was done was to pass an order in council dealing with part of it, and to refer to the terms of the peace treaty itself, in article 405, to what labour meant and to all that concerns its wellbeing; but every word and every line of that obligation is national in its character. It is not divided into nine parts. It does not concern nine provinces. It concerns them in the aggregate, and in the aggregate they become the Dominion of Canada, and therefore the obligation is national, and not provincial. The sum total of provincial Obligations can never be exercised with respect to a national matter in connection with which the country as a whole has bound itself by treaty, by piecing together piecemeal the legislation of the provinces. It must be a national exercise of the power, and that can be done only by this parliament. That is the point I desire to make and which I think concludes the question that was raised by hon. gentlemen opposite.
Let me say this The hon. gentleman was somewhat cynical with respect to the conclusions at which lawyers -arrive, and he was uncertain whether or not an opinion was held at this moment or at that moment. I do think it was unfair to suggest that a letter asking

International Labour Conventions
for a conference and dealing with the problems as put forward by the provinces, and what their attitude was, represented the attitude of the one who had extended the invitation. Obviously that can never be so. The subject matter of the discussion does not indicate the opinion of the person who extends the invitation. It would be ruinous to any conference if that were so; that is quite clear.
There is just this to be said. I did say that law was a progressive science in dealing -with the construction of our constitution. I did not for one single moment mean, as was suggested, that opinions of lawyers differ merely because they happen to be different men. But the development of civilization broadened the attitude of mind towards judicial decisions, and I quoted from the language I think of Mr. Justice Wendell Holmes, who said that common law was based not on logic but on experience. The interpretation of statutes is still governed by the same general rules to-day as it was three hundred years ago; but the broadening of the attitude of mind and outlook in the light of present day civilization is well represented by the method in which this constitution of ours has been slowly evolved and developed.
I did say that I have arrived at a conclusion, which the hon. gentleman suggests is erroneous. I am always willing to say it may be, but as far as my mind is concerned I have no doubt, and I am just as apt to be right as the hon. gentleman. I had a very substantial experience in the practice of my profession and with respect to the framework of the constitution, if he will look at the law books he will find that the position I took was supported by the privy council in all cases in which I had the privilege of arguing before them. I can say that with some degree of confidence.

I was not arguing the Nadan case on that point at all. That was the dominion. I drafted the Alberta act, with the assistance of Mr. Farley, of Edmonton, and the attorney general of that province, when the question of its constitutionality came up in the Nadan case, entrusted me with the responsibility of defending my own statute. What happened was that the dominion intervened and claimed that there was no right of appeal to the privy council. I was acting for the province, to sustain the conviction which had confiscated a Cadillac car costing about five or six thousand dollars and likewise its cargo of liquor. In the event the privy council decided the conviction was valid, the

car properly confiscated to the crown, and likewise the contents, which went to make happier the lives of some individuals. But so far as the constitutional point was concerned, that was settled by counsel representing the dominion. The present Lord Hailsham appeared for the attorney general of England. My memory is that the dominion was represented by Mr. Greene, although I am not quite certain as to that. Perhaps my hon. friend will remember.

maintopic: EIGHT HOUR DAY AND FORTY-EIGHT HOUR WEEK IN INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext: No, I am sorry I do not.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: EIGHT HOUR DAY AND FORTY-EIGHT HOUR WEEK IN INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext:
At any rate I was appearing in the interests of the province of Alberta.
You have here, Mr. Speaker, a question of first importance. We are going to enact legislation based on the ratification of a treaty, of an agreement, of a convention, and that raises a single, simple question: Did Canada under the peace treaty assume obligations? If she did, was there a convention made pursuant to that? Did Canada ratify it? If she did, in my judgment, there is no power except the parliament of Canada to deal with the question with which we are concerned.
I think it is unfortunate that we should get into a discussion as to the attitude of this party or that, or of this member or that member, with respect to these matters in the past, except as one is compelled to make answer to observations made by those opposite. This is a problem partly legal, partly social, but in any event national; and if it is national, if there should be uniformity of law, as is agreed upon by all; if there should be no conflict between provinces with respect to the terms and conditions under which they prepare goods for export; if there should be uniformity in hours of toil and cessation from toil so that there will be equality as between the provinces when goods are sold on the markets of the world, and if there should not be a mad competition-in invitations to induce manufacturers to set up their factories in this province or in that because in a particular province he may work his labour longer hours than in another-if that is wrong, as everyone agrees it must be, there is only one method by which it can be dealt with, and that is by uniformity of law. That uniformity cannot be secured by piecemeal legislation, to use the language of the books, by one province enacting an eight hour day law and another a nine hour day; by one province making limitations of this character and another of another. Rather there must be placed upon the statute books of our country a broadly conceived statute that will ensure uniformity and equality in the work with respect to the matters in which the workman is interested.

International Labour Conventions

I explained, without going into details this afternoon, that there are some of them that are so clearly not covered by the principles to which I referred that they might be regarded as purely provincial. And that was mentioned by Lord Sankey in the judgment I referred to this afternoon. I will say this, however, that each one of them, so far as we are concerned, will be dealt with on its merits as it arises. But what we are inviting this house to do is to enact legislation that will provide that a forty-eight hour law is valid in every province of confederation. I agree with what has been said, that conditions have greatly changed since 1919. Never were opportunities better to enact legislation than then. Never was the opportunity greater than at that time and following the war, during the period that my hon. friend was in office. Never, I say, was there a greater opportunity. Let us see what happened in relation to the so-called Lemieux Act. That act was passed and put on the statute books and remained there twenty odd years before it was attacked in the court. But I think it was the opinion of nine lawyers out of ten that it was invalid as it stood. At least, that was always the opinion whenever we had friendly discussions respecting the validity of statutes, and it was not until the Snider case was taken to the court of last resort that the matter was cleared up. It was suggested that we should refer the matter to the Supreme Court of Canada. But what did the privy council say? The privy council has said that the opinion of the supreme court in the matter is no better than the opinion of the law officers of the crown; and Lord Loreburne said that an opinion should not be asked for because the thing to be determined is not the validity of a hypothetical question but the validity of a concrete statute that may be enacted by the legislature, whether it be parliament or the provincial legislature. That was dealt with at some length, and Lord Sankey took this view. He said, "We cannot be draughtsmen for the Dominion of Canada. We cannot have submitted to us the whole of a statute and be asked to say what is good and what is bad therein." And in any event, the view has been held that such an opinion is no better than that of the law officers of the crown, being advisory only. He points out, further, another reason which I think is so sound that merely to mention it carries the conviction necessary in the case. Other people are bound.
This is an international obligation, and when other nations and other peoples are affected by advisory opinions and they are not before the court, it is inadvisable that such opinion be given, because it affects in any event only your own people and cannot be better, as has been said, than that of the law officers of the crown.
I was glad to hear the closing observations of the leader of the opposition that he proposed to support the passage of this resolution. One would hardly think, from the clamorous manner in which opposition was received by his adherents this afternoon, that they were anxious that anything should be passed emanating from this government. It is always one of the misfortunes of party strife that parties are unable to see that something may be beneficial to the country even though it emanates from Nazareth. The old cry, "Can any good come out of Nazareth?" was beautifully exemplified by what took place this afternoon-loud cheers and counter cheers when words were uttered against the efficiency of the legislation or the validity of the resolution-and then winding up with a magnificent display of rhetoric about undying devotion to a great cause, and the shortness of hours, so that one could hardly count the time between going to work and ceasing from work; and declaring, "We will support the measure with all our might."

I should like to offer an explanation
of a statement made by me in the house on January 24, when we were discussing the resolution of the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Spencer) with respect to the establishment of a federal health policy. In reply to the contention of the Minister of Pensions and National Health, that the country was in the main well provided with hospitals, I said:
I know there are splendid hospitals and doctors and nurses, but what does that matter when the people cannot get into the hospital without guaranteeing payment, and when they have not the money to pay for care in the hospitals? In the city of Owen Sound people have actually been kept waiting on the steps of the hospital until the hospital authorities could be assured there was going to be full pay for their hospitalization. Everyone in this house knows of innumerable instances where people have not been able to secure hospital treatment or the care of a nurse in their own home simply because they could not afford to pay for it. There are hundreds and thousands of nurses out of work in Canada who would be only too glad to take care of the sick, as the sick would be only too glad to be taken care of. But there must be dollars to bridge the chasm between unemployed nurses and uncared for sick.
I believed that the statement made by me at that time was correct, but the name of the hospital was used inadvertently. I had not intended to use the name but I did believe that the statement I made was accurate. If I may be allowed to do so, I should like in support of the statement I made, to refer to the Public Hospitals Act, 1931, passed by the Ontario legislature, a copy of which I received this morning. I would refer to the provision contained in section 18, subsection 1, on page
7.	I shall not read it. It is an amendment that was offered in 1933, which leads me to believe that there was difficulty as regards the admission of indigent patients without delay into hospitals. I had conversations with two reeves of rural municipalities last week end who said that until recently hospitals did communicate with either the clerk of the township or the reeve before admitting indigent patients into the hospitals with which those two reeves had to deal. Since that time however I received from the president of the General and Marine hospital board, Owen Sound, a letter, the tone of which I appreciate. He points out-and I want to put his statement on record-that my statement was unfair to the Owen Sound hospital. I am giving only

Privilege-Mr. Howden
two or three paragraphs which deal particularly with the matter. He said:
This notice came to me as a shock that anyone could imagine such a thing could happen, or any person ever had to wait admission on account of funds. The first duty to patients entering the hospital is to take care of the sick; rich or poor are all treated alike; no patient delayed on account of funds.
This is his statement. I would not go so far as to say that rich and poor are treated alike, but I am reading the statement he made. The next paragraph reads:
There is a necessary chart to fill out when entering, which can he done by relatives or friends if not at patient's bedside. In this chart the question of payment is asked, but all are treated alike.
I can say to you that in my experience of fifteen years as president of the Owen Sound General and Marine hospital and some years before that as member of the trustee board, I have never known of any patient being delayed in entering the hospital on account of funds. Many cases have been entered when we knew the prospects of payment were not good, also foreigners from whom we had no chance of collecting.	.
I said that that would be all, but there is really one other paragraph which should go on record. It is as follows:
This hospital is rated as an A-l standard hospital, a rating that we jealously guard, and if anything happened as stated above we would lose the high standing that we now enjoy.
The letter is signed: J. R. McLinden, president. I want to be fair to the Owen Sound hospital and state that I do regret, and that I did regret the moment after I finished speaking, not having verified the statement. which I used at the time and which I then believed to be correct.
PRIVILEGE-Mr. HOWDEN
On the orders of the day.

Before the orders of the day are called, may I say that the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) in discussing the resolution before the house a few moments ago intimated that on the occasion of my nomination I had referred to a provincial conference that was sitting at that time.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I did not say that. Look and see what I said.
He did not speak about the hon. member at all.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes, I did.
I understand that I am accused of having made remarks tending to arouse racial prejudice.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is right.

I caught just the tail end of the remarks, but I believe that was the gist of it. So far as my last nomination is concerned, it was an acclamation and my speech was exceedingly brief and merely one of appreciation of the nomination. I have a very clear and definite recollection of the speech that I made at the convention of 1930, and I believe I am justified in giving an unqualified denial to any statement that I raised racial prejudice at that time or at any time. I represent a constituency where French Roman Catholics and English Protestants are well represented-

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
speechtext: I think the hon. member has quite covered the point of order. As a matter of fact he should state the words of which he complains and then argue the point of order, but he does not seem to be very clear on that point.
I have not the printed text before me and am speaking from memory, but since I am not going to be allowed to speak, then I desire to give an unqualified denial to the statement of the Prime Minister.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I said that I would look up the newspaper and read to this chamber the report of the speech made 'by the hon. gentleman in which he warned his constituents of certain possible results that might come to them.
But the right hon. gentleman is not allowed to read newspapers, and the hon member may have been misquoted.
The Prime Minister may read a report of a speech from a newspaper, but I insist that in all my career I made no such remarks in any speech.

Sheltered employment, $50,000.
Will the minister explain this item?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: This is in connection with the vetcraft shops. We maintain at Halifax, Montreal, Toronto, Hamilton and Victoria, what are called vetcraft shops. They were started after the war, with the idea of giving sheltered employment to soldiers who were not able to hold their place on the open labour market. It is not being followed qidte as much now as in those days, but still we have the shops in those five cities. Of course they are not self supporting. They manufacture certain articles very well indeed, but their rate of production is not equal to that of men who are one hundred per cent efficient. This is to make up the loss on those shops.

Are these men able to
earn anything at all from what they produce?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Oh, yes. The proceeds from sale of products that they made last year amounted to $118,004. Since I have been in the department I went through the vetcraft shop at Montreal and was quite favourably impressed with the way they were getting on. In that shop there were about 28 men working, and they seemed happy. I looked over the goods, talked with their sales agent, and it seemed to me it was being operated very efficiently.

The reason I asked is
that we had one of these shops in Winnipeg. Unfortunately it was burned down two or three years ago, by accident no doubt, and I think some thirty men were thrown out of employment. Although many appeals were made to the government to reestablish this shop, they did not succeed. Is it the policy of the government to continue these shops, and if so, is there any possibility of reestablishing the shop we had in Winnipeg?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: No, I do not think it is the policy to start any new shops. It is not an efficient operation, but it does give employment to a number of these men. But it is my judgment, and that of the department, that no additional shops should be established.
Do I understand that any shops that might by accident be destroyed will be discontinued?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
I could not give a
definite answer to a hypothetical case. I hope nothing will happen; if it should, it would have- to be considered on its merits.

It is not fair to these men in Winnipeg. I understand they were doing very well and turning out excellent goods. The building was destroyed by fire one night, and all attempts to have it reestablished have failed. I appeal to the minister to give the matter consideration, even at this late date, and if possible to do something for these men.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
I shall be glad to
look into it.

What is the total
number employed in these shops?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
On December 31
last there were 10 at Halifax, 20 at Montreal, 47 at Toronto, 17 at Hamilton and 28 at Victoria, British Columbia.

There is no shop at
London?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: No.
Was there not a shop there at one time?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Not in my day.
What kind of men are employed in these shops? Are they partially disabled?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
Oh yes, they are all pensioners with twenty-five or thirty per cent disability, and as a rule men who have lost a good deal of their vim and energy; although in some cases when they get the chance to

Supply-Pensions and National Health
work without being pressed as they would be in ordinary commercial life they get along fairly well. Many of them are able finally to get out and take their places in industry.

How does a veteran obtain
employment in the vetcraft shops?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Our officials in these centres throughout Canada are in close touch with the returned soldiers; for instance men seeking relief or in need of medical attention on account of their pension disability come into the office. There are not many vacancies, but when one occurs whoever is in charge of the vetcraft shop intimates the fact to our official; he keeps his eye open and recommends a suitable man whom that occupation would help; and the man is taken on.

Does the minister think th?
work might be extended in order to include unemployed veterans?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I do not think it will. It filled quite a gap in the years after the war, but it is not an economical undertaking.

I received this morning a letter from a war veteran at Coronach, Saskatchewan. He had about 800 acres of land in the drought area, I understand, and he is completely ruined. He has four children, and, having been one of my schoolmates at Normal school in Montreal years ago, and hearing that I was a member of parliament, he wrote and begged me to try to obtain something for his family. 1 frankly admit that I should have seen the minister, but as the case might 'be general enough to deserve a public answer I thought it appropriate to put it before him now. This man has nothing except S48 a month pension. He said he borrowed three or four thousand dollars to buy what he needed, and his crop last year was absolutely nothing. I am sure that the minister will give me the proper information which I can send to him.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: What I suggest in a case like that is that the hon. member come down to the department and see me, and I will put him in touch with the proper official. It is hard to make a statement here on an individual case. There are many of these cases in respect to which some suggestion may be made to help. If the hon. member would see me it would be much the -better plan.

I shall excuse myself again; I knew this answer would be given. But
these veterans were allowed after the war to go farming if they were able to do so, and hundreds of them went on the land; I thought there must be many cases like this one.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Not with 800 acres.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
